| Powder preparation | Use clean gas-atomized Al and sieve gently without creating a dust cloud. Blend additions in a sealed conductive container by low-energy tumbling. Prefer two or three 20–30 mm slugs rather than one 60 mm slug to limit die-friction gradients. | Use the same powder preparation. Fill the mould incrementally with gentle vibration. Validate blending and filling because powders of different size or density can segregate. |
| Drying / degassing | Minimum: dynamic vacuum at 100–150°C for 2–4 h. Preferred qualified treatment: loose powder near 350°C (623 K) for 2–5 h, followed by cooling and transfer without air exposure. Physisorbed water evolves mainly at 100–200°C; hydroxide-related water and H₂ continue through roughly 200–450°C. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000067, pqac-00000070) | Degas loose powder before bagging with the same qualified schedule. Cool under vacuum or dry Ar, transfer in a glovebox, then evacuate and seal the bag. Reject powder after suspected water or oil contact. |
| Pressing pressure | Start at 200–300 MPa; qualify higher pressure only if handling strength is inadequate. Use double-action pressing for tall slugs or divide them into shorter pieces. Al-alloy die compacts increased from about 2.14 g/cm³ at 100 MPa to 2.57 g/cm³ at 500 MPa, although that powder contained lubricant. (pqac-00000053) | Start at 150–250 MPa with a 60 s hold; increase toward 300–400 MPa only if needed. Typical CIP practice is 200–400 MPa, while direct Al work reached 98% theoretical density at 600 MPa. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000054) |
| Press force / vessel | A 19 mm punch has an area of 283.5 mm². Required force is 56.7 kN at 200 MPa, 70.9 kN at 250 MPa, 85.1 kN at 300 MPa, 113.4 kN at 400 MPa, and 141.8 kN at 500 MPa. Use at least a guarded 150 kN press for development through 500 MPa. | Use a certified vessel with at least 25–30 mm usable bore and 80–100 mm usable depth. Rating should be at least 250 MPa for the initial recipe or 400 MPa for development at conventional CIP pressures. The vessel, closure, intensifier, tubing, and relief system must share the certified rating. |
| Dwell time | Evacuate the filled die for 2–5 min, compact gradually, hold at peak pressure for 30–60 s, and unload slowly. A longer dwell improves pressure transfer and allows gas to escape while pores remain connected. (pqac-00000046) | Hold at peak pressure for 60 s. Direct Al/Al–Ni work found that immediate decompression caused a denser surface and lower-density core, whereas a 1 min hold improved homogeneity. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005) |
| Evacuation level | Evacuate loose powder and the die cavity to ≤10 mbar absolute; ≤1 mbar is preferable with a filtered powder-rated system. Reduction from 1 bar to 10 mbar removes about 99% of equilibrated free pore gas but not oxide-bound water. Vent only with dry Ar. | Evacuate the filled bag to ≤10 mbar, preferably ≤1 mbar, while gently manipulating it to release pockets; seal under vacuum and use a second dry containment bag. A non-evacuated sealed bag compresses rather than removes the original gas. |
| Lubricant | Use no admixed lubricant or binder. If ejection requires it, use only the smallest validated external die-wall film and prevent contact with the powder. | Use no lubricant or binder. Bag motion largely eliminates internal lubrication. Avoid mould-release agents unless transfer and outgassing have been quantified. |
| Die / mould | Use a polished hardened-tool-steel or carbide-lined 19.0 mm die, preferably double-action. Include a sintered-metal powder trap, grounding, and seals outside the powder-contact region. | Use thin polyurethane, natural rubber, latex, or another compatible elastomer, preferably double-bagged. Begin with an internal former around 21–24 mm diameter and determine experimentally the oversize needed to obtain ≤19 mm after shrinkage. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000057) |
| Target green density | Target 85–90% theoretical density, equivalent to 2.30–2.43 g/cm³ for pure Al, provided measurable open porosity remains. Do not maximize density before degassing. | Target 85–90% theoretical density. If handling requires 90–95%, use only pre-degassed powder in an evacuated bag and verify gas release independently. CIP can exceed 95% at high pressure. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002) |
| Expected density and mass | At 200–300 MPa, an initial development expectation is about 2.25–2.45 g/cm³, subject to powder and tooling. At 19 mm diameter this corresponds to approximately 13–14 g at 20 mm length, 26–28 g at 40 mm, and 39–42 g at 60 mm. | At 150–250 MPa, expect approximately 2.30–2.50 g/cm³, but establish a pressure–density curve for the actual powder. Pure Al achieved 85–95% density at 103.5–138 MPa in one study and 98% at 600 MPa in another. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000063) |
| Decompression / ejection | Reduce load over 30–60 s and pause at low load before full release. Eject slowly with a supported lower punch. Inspect for end-capping, circumferential laminations, and cracks at the middle or remote end. | Decompress over at least 1–3 min and lengthen the cycle if springback cracks occur. Keep the bag contained until external fluid has been removed, then strip it over a clean tray. Low-compressibility metals may require several minutes. (pqac-00000054) |
| Dimensional acceptance | Require diameter ≤19.0 mm everywhere using a go/no-go gauge. Prefer 20–30 mm lengths. In Cu–Al compacts, increasing H/D from 0.7 to 2.12 increased maximum relative-density variation from 0.0851 to 0.1206; application to pure Al is an extrapolation. (pqac-00000046) | Require diameter ≤19.0 mm everywhere after bag removal. Reject folds, necking, taper, and closure-end bulges. Flexible-tool shrinkage must be calibrated for each bag and filling procedure. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000056) |
| Density and porosity check | Record mass, dimensions, and geometric density. Determine open porosity with a validated nonreactive immersion liquid followed by complete drying, or use helium pycnometry plus envelope density. Require batch density within ±2% relative and connected porosity if relying on in-crucible degassing. | Apply the same tests. Compare dimensions before and after CIP to detect abnormal bag restraint or leakage. During qualification, section slugs and compare top, middle, and bottom density. |
| Thermal qualification | Heat a sacrificial slug under the intended dynamic-vacuum ramp to 500°C while recording mass and pressure, preferably with H₂O/H₂ residual-gas analysis. Require reproducible mass loss and no pressure spike, swelling, cracking, spalling, or ejection. Al powders have shown about 13–25 ppm H, equivalent to 14.7–27.5 cm³ H₂ per 100 g. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000066, pqac-00000069) | Use the same qualification. Reject a part if its bag lost vacuum, changed mass unexpectedly, showed wetting or discoloration, or either containment layer was damaged. A leak into water-based fluid is disqualifying and should not be corrected by redrying. |
| Key warnings | Fit vacuum lines with grounding, a metal-powder trap, an isolation valve, and pump protection. Never vent an evacuated powder-filled die rapidly to air. Avoid moist powder, internal lubricants, tall single-action compacts, and near-full densification before degassing. Al-powder MIE can be below 1–13 mJ. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000029) | CIP adds high-pressure stored energy and a fluid-ingress failure mode. Treat either water or oil ingress as rejection. Freshly exposed Al can generate H₂ according to 2Al + 3H₂O → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂. (pqac-00000022) |


*Table: Safety-first starting recipes for producing 19 mm diameter aluminium-powder slugs by vacuum die pressing or evacuated-bag CIP. Values requiring qualification on the actual powder and equipment are presented as development ranges rather than validated production limits.*

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:

    InterventionalAssignment:

strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly

met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: We make small batches of aluminium-alloy powder by ultrasonic atomization (AMAZEMET rePOWDER, induction-heated module). We are deciding how to turn **pure aluminium powder** (gas-atomized, roughly 15-63 µm, alone or blended with alloying-element or master-alloy powders) into **green parts** that we then melt in the atomizer crucible together with solid alloy (6063 rod, 4047). We want a **pros-and-cons comparison of two consolidation routes**, (A) powder-metallurgy pressing under vacuum and (B) cold isostatic pressing (CIP), judged on **safety** first, then simplicity, speed, cost, and whether the green part will melt, coalesce and mix into the rest of the melt. Please answer from the literature, with citations (DOIs where possible), give numbers wherever the sources have them, and say explicitly which conclusions come from direct evidence for aluminium and which are extrapolated from other metals or from general PM practice.

**Set-up.** Graphite crucible (BN-coated), induction heated, 10-11 cm deep, with a sealing (stopper) rod down the middle; the melt is bottom-poured through a ~0.7 mm hBN nozzle onto a 40 kHz vibrating molybdenum plate. The charge is loaded cold. The chamber is then evacuated and back-filled with argon several times ("gas washes"), including while the charge is held at about 500 °C and still solid. It is then melted under argon at about 0.2 bar overpressure (13-20 ppm O2), set point 810-840 °C, held about 2 minutes (we may extend this to 5-10 minutes), with no mechanical stirring beyond the induction field. Charges are 170-350 g. Every piece must be under 20 mm across to fit between the stopper rod and the crucible wall, so a green part would be a slug about 19 mm in diameter and 20-60 mm long (roughly 10-40 g).

**What we already know** (our own runs, and an earlier literature review on 2026-11-02 that you do not need to repeat). Loose gas-atomized powder sealed in a 6063 cup did not consolidate in one run (AlSi10Mg) and did in another (4047); the oxide shell on each particle, plus MgO or spinel when Mg is present, keeps the molten droplets apart. Cold uniaxial pressing of Al powder reaches about 85 % relative density at about 100 MPa and 92-98 % at 250-580 MPa; it cracks the oxide but does not remove it. Pores start to close above roughly 85-90 % density, so a denser compact can seal in air, adsorbed water and water from hydrated oxide. The equipment maker warned that powder compressed inside a closed aluminium cup could eject molten metal, presumably from trapped gas. Die lubricants add gas and carbon. Cast master alloys, or an arc-melted button made from the weighed powders, were ranked above any pressed compact.

**The two routes to compare.**
- **(A) "Powder metallurgy under vacuum":** uniaxial die pressing with the die cavity evacuated before and during pressing (an evacuable die with a vacuum port and O-ring seals, or a die inside a vacuum chamber or glovebox), with or without vacuum drying or degassing of the loose powder beforehand. Please also cover the natural extensions: pressing followed by vacuum sintering or degassing, and vacuum hot pressing (for example 300-550 °C).
- **(B) Cold isostatic pressing (CIP):** powder filled into a flexible elastomer mould (polyurethane, latex, silicone or rubber bag), optionally evacuated and sealed, and pressed hydrostatically (typically 100-400 MPa) by a water-based fluid or oil. Wet-bag versus dry-bag; buying a small laboratory CIP versus sending parts to a toll-pressing service. Also the combination of A and B: powder vacuum-degassed first, sealed in an evacuated bag, then cold isostatically pressed.

**Please address:**

1. **Pros and cons of each route (and its sub-variants) for pure aluminium powder**, ideally as a table covering: process safety; safety of the green part when melted in our crucible; green density achievable versus pressure, and its uniformity (density gradients and low-density zones in uniaxially pressed slugs with height-to-diameter ratios of about 1-3, versus isostatic pressing); green strength, edge integrity and powder shedding during handling; the need for lubricants and their effect; contamination (lubricant residue, bag material, pressing fluid, die wear); dimensional control (our 20 mm limit, CIP shrinkage and shape tolerance); oxide-film disruption (does hydrostatic loading in CIP break the particle oxide films more or less than the shear in a uniaxial die?); residual gas and moisture in the part; simplicity and the skill needed; time per part and per batch; and cost (equipment capital, tooling and consumables, and toll-service pricing if published).
2. **Which route makes the safer green part to melt in the atomizer, and why.** Quantify where possible: adsorbed and chemically bound water on gas-atomized Al powder (mass %, or mL H2 per 100 g Al) and the temperatures at which it is released; the open-to-closed porosity transition for Al compacts; how much evacuating the die or the CIP bag before pressing reduces the trapped gas; and whether an open-pore green compact heated slowly through our vacuum and argon washes up to about 500 °C would degas in place before its pores close. What are the failure modes: a CIP bag leak or puncture that lets water or oil into the powder (and the hydrogen that water generates with freshly exposed Al), lubricant decomposition, trapped air expanding on heating, lamination or end-capping cracks from uniaxial pressing?
3. **Process hazards of each route** when handling fine pure Al powder: combustible-dust and ignition risks while filling dies or bags, drawing fine powder into a vacuum line or pump, venting an evacuated die to air, contact with the CIP fluid, stored energy in the high-pressure vessel, and safe practice for each (inert handling, filters, grounding, PPE).
4. **Melt-in and mixing feasibility.** Would a green part from either route (at what density) melt, coalesce and mix into a 6063 melt at 810-840 °C under argon within 2-10 minutes with only induction stirring? Does CIP versus uniaxial pressing versus vacuum hot pressing change coalescence, metal yield, dross or oxide inclusions on remelting? Use evidence from remelting Al powder compacts, chip or swarf briquettes, PM parts and foundry alloying tablets. If alloying powders (Si, Cu, Mg, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, Zr) are blended into the pure Al before pressing: segregation while filling, and exothermic reactions between Al and these powders on heating (for example the self-propagating Al-Ni, Al-Ti, Al-Fe or Al-Zr reactions in pressed compacts, and how compact density affects ignition), and whether these help or hurt safety and dissolution.
5. **A practical recipe for each route** for a 19 mm diameter by 20-60 mm slug: pressure, dwell, evacuation level, drying or degassing temperature and time, lubricant (or none), mould or die material and sizing, expected density, and how to check a part before it goes into the crucible (Archimedes density and open porosity, a weight-loss or gas-release test on heating). What press force, or what CIP vessel size and pressure rating, does this need?
6. **Recommendation:** which route, or neither, would you choose for a university lab making a few such parts per week, and when would each be the wrong choice? Compare briefly with buying cast master alloys or arc-melting a button from the weighed powders.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
Highly performance methods for cold pressing (cold die forging) of preforms from iron powder with subsequent heat treatment and producing ready parts made of powder are described in the paper. These methods allow fabricating parts with smooth surfaces and improved mechanical characteristics—porosity, tensile strength. Application of the traditional design set-up with a single-axial loading is restricted to high stresses in the dies to deform the preforms that lead to cracks formation. New powder compaction schemes by applying active friction forces (shear-enhanced compaction) make it possible to unload dies and produce high-quality parts by cold pressing. The scheme allows moving the die in the direction of the material flow with a velocity that exceeds the material flow velocity.

Abstract:
Hot isostatic pressing (HIP) technology can directly produce nearly clean shaped workpieces that meet the requirements while ensuring machining accuracy and surface quality. Usually, people use numerical simulation methods to reduce experimental costs. Generally, a uniform powder relative density distribution of about 65% is used in the simulation. However, in practical engineering, we found that even with additional tools such as vibration tables, the powder filling is not uniform. The non-uniform distribution causes uneven shrinkage of the powder and capsule after HIP. In this paper, a numerical model for HIPing of Ti-6Al-4V powder is developed to improve the prediction by comparing the uniform and non-uniform initial powder distribution. The results show that different initial relative density distributions affect the powder densification process and further affect the deformation of the capsule. It also leads to non-uniform stress distribution after HIP, which increases the risk of capsule rupture. The analysis of the numerical simulation results and the comparison with the experimental results highlights that taking into account the non-uniform powder distribution inside the capsule is vital to improve numerical results and produce near-net shape components. The maximum error of the simulation with the usual initial relative density setting of 65% is 4.2%. However, considering the uneven distribution of initial powder, the maximum error is reduced to 3.16%, and the average error is also less than 2%.

Abstract:
Powder metallurgy as a method of manufacturing and processing metals is very diverse in its technological methods. This makes it possible to obtain parts of the required quality and necessary properties. Using the methods of powder metallurgy production, specialists can produce the latest composite materials, the production of which is impossible by traditional methods. The production of machine parts and mechanisms from metal powders provides significant savings on material, due to the low consumption coefficient. Metal powders are usually manufactured in specialized factories, but sometimes they are produced directly by the consumer; in this case, the manufacturing process is built in direct accordance with the requirements of this consumer. If the powder comes from a third-party supplier, there is a need for special preparation operations, before starting production, to give the powder certain chemical and physical characteristics. Hot isostatic pressing technology is a complex technological process in which a large number of parameters affect the quality of the final product. The complexity of the GIP process lies in various thermal, physical, and mechanical interactions. In this regard, a large role is played by the processes for preparing the powder for the GIP. The article describes the main operations for the preparation of powder for hot isostatic pressing.

Abstract:
The synthesis of bulk ultrafine-grained (UFG) and nanostructured Al via cryomilling can frequently require a degassing step prior to consolidation, partly due to the large surface area of the as-milled powders. The objective of this study is to investigate the effects associated with cryomilling with stearic acid additions (as a process-control agent) on the degassing behavior of Al powders. This objective was accomplished by completing select experiments with Al-7.5Mg, Al-6.4 wt pct Al85Ni10La5, and Al-14.3 wt pct B4C. The interaction between Al and stearic acid was determined using thermal analysis combined with Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The degassing experiments were carried out under high vacuum (10−4 to ~10−6 torr) in a range from room temperature to 400 °C, with the pressure of the released gases monitored using a digital vacuum gage. The results showed that the liberation of chemisorbed water was suppressed in cryomilled Al powders and both the chemisorbed water and stearic acid were primarily released in the form of hydrogen. It was also demonstrated that under certain conditions, a nanostructure (grain size ~100 nm) can be retained following the hot vacuum degassing of cryomilled Al.

Abstract:
In powder bed fusion additive manufacturing, the powder feedstock quality is of paramount importance; as the process relies on thin layers of powder being spread and selectively melted to manufacture 3D metallic components. Conventional powder quality assessments for additive manufacturing are limited to particle morphology, particle size distribution, apparent density and flowability. However, recent studies are highlighting that these techniques may not be the most appropriate. The problem is exacerbated when studying aluminium powders as their complex cohesive behaviors dictate their flowability. The current study compares the properties of three different AlSi7Mg powders, and aims to obtain insights about the minimum required properties for acceptable powder feedstock. In addition to conventional powder characterization assessments, the powder spread density, moisture sorption, surface energy, work of cohesion, and powder rheology, were studied. This work has shown that the presence of fine particles intensifies the pick-up of moisture increasing the total particle surface energy as well as the inter-particle cohesion. This effect hinders powder flow and hence, the spreading of uniform layers needed for optimum printing. When spherical particles larger than 48 µm with a narrow particle distribution are present, the moisture sorption as well as the surface energy and cohesion characteristics are decreased enhancing powder spreadability. This result suggest that by manipulating particle distribution, size and morphology, challenging powder feedstock such as Al, can be optimized for powder bed fusion additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study presents a comprehensive characterization of recycled aluminum briquettes produced by cold pressing of Al–Si–Mg alloy machining chips, along with an evaluation of their behavior during subsequent remelting. The objective was to assess the density, porosity, chemical composition, and metallurgical yield of the briquettes before and after melting, as well as to determine their suitability for use as deoxidizing additives in steelmaking. The cold-pressed briquette (Sample A) exhibited a low density of 2.29 g.cm-³ and a porosity of 12.1%, resulting from intergranular voids and residual lubricants. After melting and resolidification (Sample B), the density increased to 2.388 g.cm-3 and the porosity decreased to 8.15%. XRF chemical analysis confirmed a high degree of elemental homogeneity after melting with no indication of segregation, while SEM–EDS microstructural analysis verified the absence of significant intermetallic phases and revealed only a thin surface oxide layer. The metallurgical yield reached 94.2% with a low dross content (2.25%). The results demonstrate that, following appropriate preprocessing and optimized compaction, recycled aluminum briquettes constitute a stable and efficient secondary aluminum material suitable for steel deoxidation, and they can significantly reduce the environmental impact of metallurgical production.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Rotary furnaces remain important in secondary aluminum production because they can process oxidized, coated, low-density, contaminated, and dross-rich feeds that are difficult to recover in conventional bath furnaces. Their flexibility creates a recovery–residue trade-off: heat, rotation, and chloride–fluoride fluxes can liberate and coalesce metal droplets, but may also increase oxidation, emissions, refractory attack, and salt-slag generation. This structured critical narrative review evaluates a coded corpus of 106 publications from 2020 to August 2026. Retrospective A–E classification was performed by one reviewer and represents interpretive judgments of industrial transferability. No level-A repeated industrial campaign with closed aluminum–salt–energy–quality balances was identified. Accordingly, the proposed nine-gate Feedstock–Flux–Furnace–Residue framework is a testable decision architecture rather than a validated control model; low-salt and salt-free strategies remain feed-specific and require prospective industrial validation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Carbothermic and aluminothermic reduction occupy complementary but non-interchangeable roles in metallurgical process design. Carbon is inexpensive, scalable, and compatible with established furnaces, but it generates CO/CO₂, promotes carbon pickup and carbide formation, and may require substantial external heat. Aluminum has a stronger oxygen affinity and releases intense exothermic heat, enabling reduction of stable oxides and production of low-carbon metals, but it increases reductant cost, generates Al₂O₃-rich slag, and raises risks from residual aluminum, aluminides, and inclusions. This critical review examines when combining both reductants is technically, economically, and environmentally justified. The corpus comprises 83 publications, including 81 from 2020–2026 and two earlier studies from 2015–2016 retained as historical evidence on self-reducing nickel agglomerates. Hybrid carbothermic–aluminothermic reduction is defined as deliberate allocation of reducible oxygen between C/CO and Al through simultaneous co-reduction, carbon-based pre-reduction followed by aluminothermic finishing, aluminum-assisted carbothermy, or staged addition within one reactor. Two descriptors are emphasized: φAl, the fraction of removed oxygen assigned to aluminum, and λR, the total reducing-equivalent ratio, distinguishing nominal charge-based values from measured oxygen balances. The review integrates thermodynamics, Boudouard chemistry, kinetics, thermal coupling, carbon activity, carbide formation, slag liquidus and viscosity, metal-droplet coalescence, reactor design, product quality, techno-economics, life-cycle implications, and scale-up. Evidence is strongest for co-reduction and secondary-feed systems; the retained corpus contains no unambiguous pilot-scale demonstration of C/CO pre-reduction followed by Al finishing. Hybridization is favored when carbon removes bulk oxygen economically and limited aluminum addition overcomes thermodynamic, kinetic, thermal, or quality constraints. The author-developed O–T–K–C–S–Q–E framework organizes conceptual feasibility gates for process selection and scale-up; it is not a validated quantitative scoring or technology-readiness tool.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Aluminum recycling is pivotal for achieving carbon neutrality and advancing the circular economy, offering significant reductions in energy use and greenhouse gas emissions compared to primary production. This review synthesizes global advances from 2020 to 2025 in scrap collection, sorting, remelting, and alloy recovery, with a focus on technological progress, sustainability metrics, and policy integration. Secondary aluminum already supplies over one-third of global demand and could surpass 50 % by 2030 with stronger segregation systems and extended producer responsibility (EPR) schemes. Innovations such as high-shear degassing, solid-state chip recycling, and chloride-free refining have improved melt quality and reduced salt-slag waste. At the same time, life-cycle assessments indicate up to 95% lower emissions compared to virgin aluminum. Persistent barriers remain—namely alloy contamination, inconsistent scrap classification, and limited traceability in informal collection networks. Regional policy experiences demonstrate that harmonized standards, mandatory recycled-content targets, and digital traceability accelerate market adaptation, whereas developing economies still face fragmented logistics and weak governance. Future directions include integrating real-time life-cycle assessment, artificial intelligence-based scrap sorting, and international alloy standards, enabling over 80% recycled content. Overall, aluminum recycling emerges as a technologically mature, economically competitive, and environmentally decisive route for decarbonizing metallurgical production and supporting the global energy transition.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The Ni-Al system contains five intermetallic compounds, out of which NiAl and Ni3Al have received the vast majority of scientific and industrial interest over the past few decades. Ni3Al is of major interest due to its unique properties, including a yield strength that increases with temperature. The combustion synthesis (CS) process for producing Ni3Al from elemental powders of nickel and aluminum offers a low thermal budget and rapid processing, as well as purer products. This paper reviews the fundamentals of CS as applied to Ni3Al and its composites, and focuses on research over the past 25 years, including mechanically and electrically activated combustion synthesis and combined combustion synthesis and bulk deformation processes to produce high-density products. Several new directions are suggested for future research in the field.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The present article investigates the fabrication of oxide dispersion strengthened (ODS) ferritic stainless steel (FSS). Three different ODS alloys with three different Al contents were fabricated, where the presence of Al-based oxides play a crucial role in determining the size of the oxide particles. Due to Ostwald ripening, the samples with Al show coarser oxide particles compared to the alloy without Al, which hampers the density of the fabricated samples and, hence, have reduced hardness levels. The present results suggest that the composition of the oxide present in ODS plays a crucial role in determining the properties of these samples.

Abstract:
In recent years, closed-cell porous Aluminum (Al) has drawn increasing attention, particularly in the applications requiring reduced weight and energy absorption capability such as in the automotive and aerospace industries. In the present work, porous Al with closed-cell structure was successfully fabricated by powder metallurgy technique using PMMA as a space holder. The effects of the amount of PMMA powder on the porosity, density, microstructure and compressive behaviors of the porous specimens were systematically evaluated. The results showed that closed-cell porous Al having different porosities (12%–32%) and densities (1.6478 g/cm3, 1.5125 g/cm3 and 1.305 g/cm3) could be produced by varying the amount of PMMA (20–30 wt %). Meanwhile, the compressive behavior results demonstrated that the plateau stress decreased and the energy absorption capacity increased with increasing amount of PMMA. However, the maximum energy absorption capacity was achieved in the closed-cell porous Al with the addition of 25 wt % PMMA. Therefore, fabrication of closed-cell porous Al using 25 wt % PMMA is considered as the optimal condition in the present study since the resultant closed-cell porous Al possessed good combinations of porosity, density and plateau stress, as well as energy absorption capacity.

It states that cold isostatic pressing (CIP) applies compaction pressure through a pressurized fluid, with the powder held in a flexible mold. CIP produces a highly uniform density distribution, implying minimal density gradients throughout the compact, but it is slow and gives poor dimensional tolerances. Uniaxial die compaction places powder in a rigid die and applies pressure through punches, either from one direction (single action) or from both top and bottom (double action). Die-wall friction reduces the transmitted pressure along the compact, creating density gradients. In single-action pressing, the bottom has the lowest pressure and density; in double-action pressing, pressure is minimized near the center, known as the density split. Thus, the excerpt supports the conclusion that CIP is more uniform, while uniaxial pressing has greater density variation, but specific pressure-density values and a quantitative comparison for aluminum are absent from these pages.

Dross was approximately 11.7–13.5% of briquette mass under argon, versus 32.5–34.8% without protection. Furnace type also mattered: induction melting gave about 83.3–85.1% incorporation and 9.6–11.4% dross, whereas resistance melting gave 62.5–68.8% incorporation and 27.1–32.3% dross under the reported conditions. At 800 °C, incorporation was 79.5–81.8% with 14.1–15.5% dross; at 900 °C it was 82.6–84.8% with 11.7–12.7% dross; and at 950 °C it was 82.2–85.2% with 11.6–13.4% dross. ## pqac-00000022

From text 'reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 6-7'.

Nicholas S. Reding and Mark B. Shiflett. Metal dust explosion hazards: a technical review. Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research, 57:11473-11482, Aug 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.8b02465, doi:10.1021/acs.iecr.8b02465. This article has 56 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides key aluminum dust explosibility parameters but does not give a numerical minimum explosible concentration (MEC); it states that KSt, MEC, and minimum ignition energy (MIE) increase as particle size decreases. For micrometer-sized aluminum powder, reported values include KSt as high as 1100 bar·m/s, maximum explosion overpressure as high as 12.9 bar, and MIE as low as less than 1 mJ. Larger aluminum flakes can still produce a KSt of 600 bar·m/s, showing that particle size alone does not define the hazard; particle shape, dust nature, and dispersity are also important. The excerpt describes moisture-related hydrogen generation: adsorbed water reacts with aluminum according to 2Al + 3H2O → Al2O3 + 3H2. Once the oxide shell is broken, the resulting hydrogen adds another fuel source and can increase reactivity. Saturating the atmosphere immediately before ignition reduced the maximum pressure-rise rate in one test, whereas long-term humidity exposure allowed water adsorption and produced very high pressure-rise rates. The excerpt discusses turbulence and dispersion effects but does not provide specific recommendations concerning grounding, inerting, or personal protective equipment (PPE).

The excerpt concerns Al-Ti, specifically SHS of TiAl, Ti3Al, and TiAl3, and does not provide data for Al-Ni compacts. Because Ti-Al reactions have relatively low exothermicity, conventional ignition by a hot tungsten wire was unsuccessful without preheating; surface reactions could extinguish before becoming self-sustaining. The study therefore used induction heating to rapidly preheat and ignite the compact, with power switched off after combustion began. It cites an empirical criterion that self-sustaining combustion generally requires an adiabatic temperature above 1800 K, while direct TiAl synthesis has a calculated adiabatic temperature of 1518 K. Preheating raises the effective adiabatic temperature and enables propagation, while rapid preheating near ignition minimizes undesired phases. Green density was experimentally varied from 55% to 75% relative density, and its effects on ignition time, combustion-wave velocity, and combustion temperature were investigated, although the provided excerpt does not state the direction or numerical magnitude of those effects. The experiments used pressed elemental Ti-Al powders under flowing argon. The excerpt indicates a potential hazard relevant to pressed aluminum/transition-metal powder compacts: localized ignition may initiate a highly exothermic combustion front, though insufficient preheating can instead cause incomplete propagation or extinction. The reaction caused a rapid temperature rise after electrical power was switched off; the maximum combustion temperature was obtained from temperature-time curves. ## pqac-00000038

From text 'carney1990anxrayphotoelectron pages 86-90'.

TJ Carney. An x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy study of rapidly solidified aluminium alloy powders. Unknown journal, 1990.

The excerpt does not provide specific vacuum hot-pressing or vacuum-sintering processing parameters such as temperature, applied pressure, holding time, or achieved density. It does, however, explain why oxide films and degassing are important during consolidation of aluminum powder. Aluminum powder surfaces can hydrate in water-containing atmospheres; hydroxide layers grow with exposure time and relative humidity, although the measured layers remain thin compared with the approximately 5.0 nm average oxide thickness reported for the studied powders. During heating, degassing removes physically adsorbed water and hydrated oxide products. The cited reactions release water and hydrogen, with hydrogen evolution becoming prominent at roughly 350–400°C. Incomplete removal before consolidation can produce voids and blisters, including potentially during subsequent service. Degassing may also promote oxide-skin breakup through recrystallization reactions, thereby facilitating consolidation. The degassing temperature must balance these effects: excessively low temperatures risk retained water, hydrogen, blistering, and void formation, whereas excessively high temperatures can cause grain growth, precipitate coarsening, or unwanted precipitate formation. The excerpt emphasizes that oxygen distribution and the state of the oxide may matter more than total oxygen content. It contains no direct discussion of vacuum-sintered aluminum compact density or a quantified mechanism for oxide disruption under vacuum hot pressing.

## pqac-00000039

From text 'sweet2014advancedsinteringtechniques pages 55-61'.

G Sweet. Advanced sintering techniques of aluminum: spark plasma sintering. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt concerns spark plasma sintering rather than conventional vacuum hot pressing or vacuum sintering, but it provides relevant aluminum-powder processing evidence. Aluminum and Al–0.4Mg powders were processed under 50 MPa; density increased with sintering temperature and reached approximately 99.97% at 600°C. For pure Al, oxide-layer disruption and densification were associated primarily with mechanical fracture, requiring about 600°C for full densification. A small magnesium addition promoted chemical reduction of the surface oxide and enabled full densification at a temperature roughly 100°C lower. Applied pressure and sintering temperature were identified as the dominant variables, while hold time and heating rate had comparatively minor effects. SPS also reduced surface impurities: hydrogen fell to roughly 5–10 ppm at 600°C, while oxygen was appreciably reduced but remained in the compact, with magnesium influencing the residual oxygen level. The oxide film is described as hydrated, containing water-related species such as H2O, hydrated alumina, or aluminum hydroxide. Under low pressure and moderate temperature, these hydrate phases can decompose spontaneously; gaseous products escape through interconnected porosity and are removed by a vacuum pump. Thus, vacuum-assisted degassing can reduce hydrogen and oxygen-bearing surface contamination during consolidation, although the excerpt does not provide separate vacuum-hot-pressing or vacuum-sintering density data.

## pqac-00000040

From text 'carney1990anxrayphotoelectron pages 90-95'.

The excerpt does not provide specific vacuum hot-pressing temperatures, applied pressures, or a numerical density achieved, nor does it give a detailed account of vacuum sintering of aluminum powder compacts. It does explain the governing mechanisms. Hot pressing or HIP supplies sufficient material flow to disrupt oxide films locally, but generally does not disperse the oxide; mechanical work is therefore needed to break up and redistribute the film so metallic interparticle bonding can form and oxide stringers at prior particle boundaries (PPBs) do not create weak paths. Complete removal of porosity is considered essential because pores act as crack initiation and stress-concentration sites. Degassing should balance gas removal against microstructural degradation, including grain growth and coarsening of intermetallics; excessive temperature can also cause loss of volatile magnesium or zinc. For an Al-Fe-Ce alloy, temperature was the critical parameter: complete degassing required heating to the maximum temperature, while longer treatment at lower temperatures was ineffective. Vacuum is necessary because degassing in air does not fully remove evolved gases. Air-atomized powders can contain hydrated oxide, whereas inert-gas powders mainly have adsorbed water and are easier to degas; re-exposure after degassing causes water readsorption. The excerpt also reports that increasing dynamic-compaction energy increased density and hardness, with evidence of full interparticle bonding in one case.

## 1. Numerical Simulation of Densification of Cu–Al Mixed Metal Powder during Axial Compaction

Abstract:
The densification mechanism of Cu–Al mixed metal powder during a double-action die compaction was investigated by numerical simulation. The finite element method and experiment were performed to compare the effect of the forming method, such as single-action die compaction and double-action die compaction, on the properties of compact. The results showed that the latter could significantly raise the densification rate and were in good agreement with Van Der Zwan–Siskens compaction equation. The effects of the different initial packing structures on the properties of the compact were studied. The results showed that a high-performance compact could be obtained using a dense initial packing structure at a given compaction pressure. Additionally, the effects of the Al content and compaction pressure on the relative density and stress distribution were analyzed. It was observed that, with an increase in the Al content at a given compaction pressure, the relative density of the compact increased, whereas the stress decreased. Furthermore, when the Al content was fixed, the relative density and stress increased with increasing compaction pressure. The relationship between the relative density and the compaction pressure under different friction conditions was characterized and fitted according to the Van Der Zwan–Siskens compaction equation. The influence mechanisms of die wall friction on the compaction behavior were investigated. It was revealed that friction is a key factor that causes the inhomogeneity of the powder flow and stress distribution. Finally, the effects of the dwell time and height–diameter ratio on the densification behavior were analyzed, and it was found that an increase in the dwell time promoted the densification process, whereas an increase of the height–diameter ratio could hinder the process.

Abstract:
In this paper, the analysis method which coupled discrete element method (DEM) and finite element method (FEM) is used to simulate the double compaction of random packing of Cu and Al composite powders with multiple particle sizes. Cu and Al composite powders with varying particle size ratios from 1:2 to 1:5 were generated by DEM and then imported to MSC. Marc software to construct FEM analysis. The effects of metal ratios, compaction pressure and size ratios on the relative density and von Mises stress of the compact were studied. The results show that the average relative density of the compact increases with the Al content, and the stress decreases. The stress in the Cu particle is particularly higher than that in the Al particle, mainly because the contact normal force of the Cu particle is nearly parallel at each contact surface. Therefore, the phenomenon of stress concentration is easier to occur within copper particles. When Al content is 30wt%, the particle size difference enhances densification efficiency by up to 12.3%, as evidenced by an initial relative density increase from 0.7915 to 0.8047, primarily due to smaller Cu particles effectively filling interparticle voids. When the compaction pressure is fixed, the average relative density of the compact with the particle size ratio 1:5 is higher than the others, and the contact forces inside the particles significantly decrease.

## pqac-00000054

From text 'meluch2010warmcompactionof pages 51-58'.

L Meluch. Warm compaction of aluminium alloy alumix 123. Unknown journal, 2010.

The excerpt describes cold isostatic pressing (CIP) as a process in which powder is enclosed in a flexible mould and compacted by pressurised fluid, rather than by direct uniaxial die loading. The mould must behave like a liquid under high pressure while retaining the required shape at normal pressure. CIP moulds are made from rubber, neoprene, urethane, or other elastomeric materials, and the pressure medium may be oil, water, or glycerine. The stated typical CIP working pressure is 200–400 MPa, with pressure maintained for only a few seconds; for low-compressibility metals, decompression may take several minutes to reduce cracking caused by elastic springback. Because the mould moves with the powder during densification, friction is minimized and pressure acts nearly uniformly from all directions. This produces comparatively uniform density, higher green strength, and allows lower pressure for a given density than die compaction. However, flexible tooling provides less precise dimensional control than rigid die pressing. The excerpt does not distinguish wet-bag from dry-bag CIP, discuss contamination from the bag or fluid, quantify shrinkage, or explain oxide-film disruption mechanisms compared with uniaxial pressing.

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a comprehensive pros-and-cons comparison table for Route A (vacuum-assisted uniaxial die pressing) versus Route B (cold isostatic pressing / CIP) for consolidating pure aluminum powder into green parts for remelting in an ultrasonic atomizer. The table should have columns for: Criterion, Route A (Vacuum Uniaxial Pressing), Route B (Cold Isostatic Pressing), and which is preferred. Rows should cover: Process safety during pressing, Safety of green part on remelting, Green density achievable, Density uniformity, Green strength/handling, Lubricant need and contamination, CIP bag/fluid contamination risk, Oxide film disruption, Residual gas and moisture, Dimensional control, Simplicity/skill needed, Time per part, Equipment capital cost, and Overall recommendation. Include specific numbers where available from the literature."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Criterion | Route A — Vacuum uniaxial pressing | Route B — Cold isostatic pressing (CIP) | Preferred |
|---|---|---|---|
| Process safety during pressing | Powder can remain in an evacuable rigid die or inert glovebox, limiting transfers. Hazards include dust entrainment into the vacuum line, electrostatic ignition, pinch loads, and dust release during venting. Reported Al-powder values span MIE <1–13 mJ, MEC 45–170 g/m³, KSt 162–1100 bar·m/s, and Pmax 8–12.9 bar. Use grounded conductive equipment, filtered vacuum lines, and slow inert-gas venting. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029) | Adds high-pressure stored energy and more powder handling. A punctured wet bag can expose Al to water or oil. Water contacting exposed Al can generate hydrogen by 2Al + 3H₂O → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂. Use an evacuated, leak-tested, double-contained bag and an oil rather than water medium where practicable. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000057) | **A**, if engineered for combustible metal powder. |
| Safety of green part during remelting | Evacuating the loose bed before pressing removes much free pore gas, but high-density pressing can isolate remaining air, water, or lubricant. A lubricant-free, measurably open-pore compact that is slowly heated under dynamic vacuum is preferable to a nearly closed, un-degassed compact. | An evacuated dry bag can remove free gas before densification and CIP avoids weak low-density zones. A leaking wet bag can introduce water or oil; a sealed but non-evacuated bag merely compresses the original gas. | **A by default**; **B only with an evacuated, dry, leak-tested bag**. |
| Green density achievable | Direct Al-alloy evidence: single-action pressing produced about 2.14 g/cm³ at 100 MPa and 2.57 g/cm³ at 500 MPa. That powder contained lubricant, so it is not a pure-Al calibration. Vacuum changes gas inventory more than the pressure–density curve. (pqac-00000053) | Direct Al evidence: initial packing near 48% theoretical density reached 98% at 600 MPa; other pure-Al/Al–Ni work exceeded 95% at sufficiently high pressure. Typical CIP practice is 200–400 MPa. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000054) | **B** for maximum density, although maximum density before degassing is not the safest target. |
| Density uniformity | Die-wall friction attenuates pressure. Single-action pressing leaves the remote end least dense; double-action pressing moves the minimum toward mid-height. In Cu–Al compacts, raising H/D from 0.7 to 2.12 increased maximum relative-density difference from 0.0851 to 0.1206; application to pure Al is an extrapolation. (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000052) | Hydrostatic loading and the moving elastomer wall provide much better uniformity. Direct Al–Ni/pure-Al work found that a 1 min pressure dwell produced good homogeneity, whereas immediate decompression produced a dense surface and lower-density core. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005) | **B**, especially for long slugs with H/D around 2–3. |
| Green strength, edge integrity, and shedding | Good at adequate pressure, but tall slugs are vulnerable to laminations, end-capping, weak central regions, and ejection damage. Rigid tooling gives clean edges. | Usually higher and more uniform handling strength, without rigid-die ejection. Bag wrinkles and rounded edges are possible; slow decompression may be needed to prevent springback cracking. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000058) | **B** for handling; **A** for precise edges. |
| Lubricant need and contamination | Die friction encourages lubricant use, but internal wax or stearate adds carbon and gas. For remelting, use no admixed lubricant; if unavoidable, apply the minimum external die-wall film and validate its removal. | Normally needs no internal lubricant because the bag moves with the powder, avoiding wax decomposition and carbon pickup. | **B**. |
| Bag or pressure-fluid contamination | No bag or pressure fluid. Possible contamination comes from die wear, vacuum grease, O-rings, pump backstreaming, or external die lubricant. | Possible elastomer fragments, mould-release residue, oil permeation, or catastrophic fluid ingress. Literature describes rubber, neoprene, or urethane moulds with water, oil, glycerine, or boron oil. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000057) | **A**. |
| Oxide-film disruption | Axial plastic flow and die-wall shear can crack native oxide locally, but do not remove it. | Hydrostatic compression deforms particles but produces less macroscopic shear. It probably fractures oxide at contacts, but direct evidence that ordinary CIP disrupts pure-Al oxide more effectively than die pressing was not found. | **A, slightly**, for cold oxide cracking; the distinction is uncertain. |
| Residual gas and moisture | Direct evacuation of the loose bed removes free interstitial gas. Al powders have shown about 13–25 ppm H, equivalent to approximately 14.7–27.5 cm³ H₂ per 100 g, mainly associated with water on the oxide. Physisorbed water evolves mainly near 100–200°C; hydroxide-related water and H₂ evolve broadly through 200–450°C. Hydrated oxide transforms near 350°C (623 K). (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000067, pqac-00000069) | Evacuating the bag removes free gas but not oxide-bound water. Fluid exposure can add moisture after drying. A non-evacuated bag traps the initial gas inventory. | **A**, unless B uses vacuum-degassed powder and dry evacuated-bag sealing. |
| Dimensional control and 20 mm limit | Best control. A nominal 19 mm rigid die produces a near-final diameter; springback should be calibrated and every slug checked with a go/no-go gauge. | Flexible-tool shrinkage depends on fill density, bag stiffness, closure geometry, and powder flow. Curvature, taper, and wrinkles are possible, and oversize mould dimensions must be established experimentally. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000056) | **A**. |
| Simplicity and skill | Straightforward if a guarded press exists, although vacuum ports, filters, inert venting, seals, and preferably double-action tooling add complexity. | Wet-bag CIP requires bag filling, evacuation, sealing, vessel loading, pressure cycling, controlled decompression, stripping, and leak inspection. Dry-bag equipment is faster but difficult to justify for a few parts weekly. | **A** in a university laboratory; toll CIP is preferable to buying a unit for trials. |
| Time per part or batch | Filling, evacuation, pressing, decompression, and ejection can take minutes. Several short slugs are easier than one H/D≈3 slug. Separate thermal degassing dominates total time. | Pressure hold may be seconds to 1 min, but bag preparation and vessel cycling dominate; decompression may take several minutes. Several bags can be processed together. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000054) | **A** for one-offs; **B** for batches. |
| Equipment capital and consumables | Lowest likely capital if a hydraulic press is available. Requires a hardened die, punches, vacuum hardware, filtration, and guarded/inert venting. Rigid tooling has low recurring consumable cost. | A 200–400 MPa vessel, intensifier, interlocked enclosure, inspection program, and disposable bags impose substantial capital and operating cost. Wet-bag tooling is cheaper but labor intensive. No reliable published toll-service price was found. | **A**; use toll CIP for occasional development work. |

{"answer": "## Vacuum-Assisted Uniaxial Die Pressing (Route A) versus Cold Isostatic Pressing (Route B) for Producing Aluminium-Powder Green Parts for Ultrasonic Atomizer Remelting

### 1. Pros-and-Cons Comparison

The following table provides a safety-first, criterion-by-criterion comparison of the two consolidation routes and their sub-variants, based on direct aluminium evidence where available and on general powder-metallurgy practice where noted.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2. Which Route Produces the Safer Green Part to Melt, and Why

**Adsorbed and chemically bound water.** Gas-atomized aluminium powder carries an amorphous hydrated oxide layer approximately 2–10 nm thick (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000072). Total hydrogen content is typically 13–25 ppm (by weight), equivalent to approximately 14.7–27.5 cm³ H₂ per 100 g of powder, which is 50–100 times higher than that of a degassed casting (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000011). Nearly all of this hydrogen originates from water that is physically adsorbed or chemically bonded as hydroxides in the surface oxide layer (pqac-00000066). Physisorbed water is released broadly around 100–200 °C; water associated with hydroxide decomposition (Al₂O₃·3H₂O → Al₂O₃·H₂O → γ-Al₂O₃) evolves over approximately 150–500 °C, with a major transition near 350 °C (623 K) (pqac-00000067, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000010). Hydrogen from the reaction 2Al + 3H₂O → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂ evolves sharply above approximately 350–400 °C and peaks near 450 °C (725 K for pure Al) (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000070). The optimum vacuum degassing temperature for Al powder consolidation is identified as 623 K (350 °C); for applications requiring minimal blistering, temperatures above 673 K (400 °C) are recommended (pqac-00000010).

**Open-to-closed porosity transition.** As aluminium compacts are pressed above approximately 85–90% relative density, pores begin to disconnect and become closed, trapping whatever gas remains inside (pqac-00000058). This is the critical safety threshold: a compact pressed to, say, 95% density without prior degassing can seal in air, adsorbed water, and hydroxide-derived hydrogen. When subsequently heated past 350–450 °C, water reacts with freshly exposed aluminium to generate hydrogen gas in a sealed cavity, potentially building enough pressure to eject molten metal—consistent with the equipment maker's warning.

**Evacuating the die versus evacuating the CIP bag.** Evacuating the die cavity to ≤10 mbar before pressing removes approximately 99% of the equilibrated free interstitial gas (atmospheric pressure to 10 mbar represents a 100-fold reduction). However, evacuation does not remove oxide-bound water, which requires thermal treatment. A CIP bag can also be evacuated before sealing, but a sealed but non-evacuated bag merely compresses the original gas inventory. A wet-bag CIP leak introduces water or oil directly into the powder, potentially exposing freshly cracked aluminium surfaces to water—a severe hydrogen-generation hazard (pqac-00000022).

**Degassing during the vacuum/argon-wash cycle.** An open-pore green compact (below roughly 85–90% density) heated slowly through the vacuum and argon washes up to 500 °C would indeed lose most of its physisorbed and hydroxide-bound water before pore closure occurs at the melting point, because the dehydration temperatures (100–500 °C) fall well below the aluminium solidus (660 °C). The interconnected porosity at 80–88% density permits gas transport to external surfaces under dynamic vacuum. This is a significant safety advantage over a nearly fully dense compact that cannot degas in situ.

Route B adds: (v) CIP bag leak or puncture that admits water or oil to the powder, generating hydrogen on freshly exposed Al surfaces; (vi) residual bag or mould-release material contributing organic contamination; and (vii) high-pressure stored-energy release in the event of vessel failure. ### 3. Process Hazards

**Aluminium dust explosion characteristics.** Aluminium powder in the 15–63 µm range is classified in Dust Hazard Class 3 (St3), with reported explosion parameters including: minimum ignition energy (MIE) as low as <1 mJ and typically 3–13 mJ; minimum explosible concentration (MEC) of 45–170 g/m³; deflagration index (K_St) of 162–1100 bar·m/s depending on particle size, shape, and test conditions; and maximum explosion pressure (P_max) of 8–12.9 bar (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000027).
