By analogy with briquette remelting, metal yield of approximately 90–95% is a reasonable expectation for a pre-degassed, lubricant-free compact under argon, with the principal loss being oxide-skin dross (extrapolated from chip-briquette data). Achieving yield at the higher end of this range requires minimising re-oxidation during loading and melting.

**CIP versus uniaxial versus vacuum hot pressing.** The consolidation method primarily affects remelting through its influence on residual gas and porosity distribution. A uniformly porous CIP compact and a uniaxially pressed compact with some density gradient should both melt and coalesce, but the CIP compact may break up more uniformly. A vacuum-hot-pressed compact approaching full density would melt in the same manner as a solid piece of aluminium—no gas ejection risk—but vacuum hot pressing at 550 °C and 175–245 MPa for hours is disproportionate effort for a simple remelt feedstock (pqac-00000064, pqac-00000065).

**Alloying-powder blends: segregation and exothermic reactions.** If Si, Cu, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, or Zr powders are blended into the Al before pressing, segregation during die filling (density- and size-driven) must be controlled by careful blending and incremental filling. More critically, binary Al–Ni compacts can undergo self-propagating high-temperature synthesis (SHS) with ignition near 640 °C for Ni+Al→Ni₃Al, well below the atomizer melt temperature of 810–840 °C (pqac-00000033). Al–Ti compacts have a lower exothermicity (adiabatic temperature ~1518 K for TiAl) and may not self-sustain without preheating, but the onset of solid-state reaction is composition- and density-dependent (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). The optimal compact green density for SHS is approximately 60–70% of theoretical; higher density improves particle contact and can raise combustion temperature (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033). Moisture in compacts promotes porosity and can slow or disrupt the combustion wave (pqac-00000037). For the user's application, SHS reactions are a potential safety hazard during the slow heating ramp: if the compact reaches the ignition temperature before being submerged in the melt, a runaway exotherm could eject material. **Use of Ni, Ti, Fe, or Zr elemental powders blended with Al in a pressed compact is therefore strongly discouraged for this application.** Master-alloy powders or pre-alloyed powders, where the elements are already in solid solution or as stable intermetallics, do not support SHS and are safer.

### 5. Practical Recipes

The following table provides starting recipes for each route, with specific pressures, forces, evacuation levels, and quality checks.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 6. Recommendation

For a university laboratory making a few 19 mm × 20–60 mm aluminium-powder slugs per week for remelting in an ultrasonic atomizer:

**Route A (vacuum-assisted uniaxial die pressing) is recommended over Route B (CIP).** Route A is simpler, requires less capital (a guarded hydraulic press, hardened die, and vacuum hardware versus a certified high-pressure CIP vessel and ancillaries), introduces no fluid-contact failure mode, and provides better dimensional control for the tight 19 mm clearance. With lubricant-free pressing at 200–300 MPa after vacuum drying of the powder, targeting 85–90% theoretical density with retained open porosity, the compact can degas in situ during the atomizer's vacuum and argon-wash cycles before its pores close at the melting point. The compact should be pressed as short slugs (H/D ≤ 1.5, i.e. ≤ 28 mm long) using double-action punches to minimise density gradients (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000052). Every slug should be verified by Archimedes density and a go/no-go gauge before loading.

**When Route A is the wrong choice:** (i) if a tall slug (H/D > 2) is required and density uniformity is critical—CIP is then better for structural uniformity, but use pre-degassed powder in a dry evacuated bag; (ii) if the laboratory already has access to a CIP facility or toll-pressing service and not a suitable press, sending occasional parts out for CIP may be faster than building tooling in-house.

**When Route B is the wrong choice:** (i) if no CIP facility is available and the cost of a vessel is not justified for a few parts per week; (ii) if only water-based CIP fluid is available, because any bag leak exposes Al powder to water; (iii) if the operator cannot reliably verify bag integrity and vacuum seal before and after pressing.

**When neither route is the best choice:** Cast master alloys or an arc-melted button from the weighed elemental charges remain safer and more reliable than any green pressed compact. A fully pre-melted and solidified charge piece contains no trapped gas, no adsorbed water, no individual particle oxide shells, and no risk of powder ejection—it simply remelts. The trade-off is that arc melting requires an arc furnace and produces only one composition per melt, while pressing is a room-temperature process that can incorporate custom powder blends. For standard alloy compositions (6063, 4047) where commercial master alloys are available, the recommendation is to **prefer cast or arc-melted charge pieces over either pressed-powder route**, and to reserve powder pressing for compositions where no suitable master alloy exists and where the added risks can be justified and managed.

### Evidence Basis and Limitations

Direct aluminium-specific evidence is available for: green density versus pressure in CIP (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000001); degassing temperatures and hydrogen content of gas-atomised Al powder (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000066, pqac-00000067, pqac-00000068, pqac-00000069); Al-powder explosion parameters (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029); SHS ignition in Al–Ni and Al–Ti compacts (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000032); vacuum hot pressing of Al composites (pqac-00000064, pqac-00000065); and remelting of Al chip briquettes (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). Density-gradient data for uniaxially pressed compacts at various H/D ratios are extrapolated from Cu–Al mixed-powder simulations (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000048); general CIP descriptions are from PM textbook-level sources applied to aluminium (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000056); and the specific behavior of a pressed Al-powder green compact during remelting in a small induction-heated crucible has not been directly studied in the published literature and is inferred from briquette remelting studies and PM degassing work. The oxide-disruption mechanism in CIP versus uniaxial pressing for pure aluminium powder has not been experimentally compared in any study identified in this review; the conclusion that uniaxial pressing introduces slightly more shear-induced oxide cracking is a reasonable inference from general PM principles but is not validated for this system."}

We make small batches of aluminium-alloy powder by ultrasonic atomization (AMAZEMET rePOWDER, induction-heated module). We are deciding how to turn **pure aluminium powder** (gas-atomized, roughly 15-63 µm, alone or blended with alloying-element or master-alloy powders) into **green parts** that we then melt in the atomizer crucible together with solid alloy (6063 rod, 4047). We want a **pros-and-cons comparison of two consolidation routes**, (A) powder-metallurgy pressing under vacuum and (B) cold isostatic pressing (CIP), judged on **safety** first, then simplicity, speed, cost, and whether the green part will melt, coalesce and mix into the rest of the melt. Please answer from the literature, with citations (DOIs where possible), give numbers wherever the sources have them, and say explicitly which conclusions come from direct evidence for aluminium and which are extrapolated from other metals or from general PM practice.

**Set-up.** Graphite crucible (BN-coated), induction heated, 10-11 cm deep, with a sealing (stopper) rod down the middle; the melt is bottom-poured through a ~0.7 mm hBN nozzle onto a 40 kHz vibrating molybdenum plate. The charge is loaded cold. The chamber is then evacuated and back-filled with argon several times ("gas washes"), including while the charge is held at about 500 °C and still solid. It is then melted under argon at about 0.2 bar overpressure (13-20 ppm O2), set point 810-840 °C, held about 2 minutes (we may extend this to 5-10 minutes), with no mechanical stirring beyond the induction field. Charges are 170-350 g. Every piece must be under 20 mm across to fit between the stopper rod and the crucible wall, so a green part would be a slug about 19 mm in diameter and 20-60 mm long (roughly 10-40 g).

**What we already know** (our own runs, and an earlier literature review on 2026-11-02 that you do not need to repeat). Loose gas-atomized powder sealed in a 6063 cup did not consolidate in one run (AlSi10Mg) and did in another (4047); the oxide shell on each particle, plus MgO or spinel when Mg is present, keeps the molten droplets apart. Cold uniaxial pressing of Al powder reaches about 85 % relative density at about 100 MPa and 92-98 % at 250-580 MPa; it cracks the oxide but does not remove it. Pores start to close above roughly 85-90 % density, so a denser compact can seal in air, adsorbed water and water from hydrated oxide. The equipment maker warned that powder compressed inside a closed aluminium cup could eject molten metal, presumably from trapped gas. Die lubricants add gas and carbon. Cast master alloys, or an arc-melted button made from the weighed powders, were ranked above any pressed compact.

**The two routes to compare.**
- **(A) "Powder metallurgy under vacuum":** uniaxial die pressing with the die cavity evacuated before and during pressing (an evacuable die with a vacuum port and O-ring seals, or a die inside a vacuum chamber or glovebox), with or without vacuum drying or degassing of the loose powder beforehand. Please also cover the natural extensions: pressing followed by vacuum sintering or degassing, and vacuum hot pressing (for example 300-550 °C).
- **(B) Cold isostatic pressing (CIP):** powder filled into a flexible elastomer mould (polyurethane, latex, silicone or rubber bag), optionally evacuated and sealed, and pressed hydrostatically (typically 100-400 MPa) by a water-based fluid or oil. Wet-bag versus dry-bag; buying a small laboratory CIP versus sending parts to a toll-pressing service. Also the combination of A and B: powder vacuum-degassed first, sealed in an evacuated bag, then cold isostatically pressed.

**Please address:**

1. **Pros and cons of each route (and its sub-variants) for pure aluminium powder**, ideally as a table covering: process safety; safety of the green part when melted in our crucible; green density achievable versus pressure, and its uniformity (density gradients and low-density zones in uniaxially pressed slugs with height-to-diameter ratios of about 1-3, versus isostatic pressing); green strength, edge integrity and powder shedding during handling; the need for lubricants and their effect; contamination (lubricant residue, bag material, pressing fluid, die wear); dimensional control (our 20 mm limit, CIP shrinkage and shape tolerance); oxide-film disruption (does hydrostatic loading in CIP break the particle oxide films more or less than the shear in a uniaxial die?); residual gas and moisture in the part; simplicity and the skill needed; time per part and per batch; and cost (equipment capital, tooling and consumables, and toll-service pricing if published).
2. **Which route makes the safer green part to melt in the atomizer, and why.** Quantify where possible: adsorbed and chemically bound water on gas-atomized Al powder (mass %, or mL H2 per 100 g Al) and the temperatures at which it is released; the open-to-closed porosity transition for Al compacts; how much evacuating the die or the CIP bag before pressing reduces the trapped gas; and whether an open-pore green compact heated slowly through our vacuum and argon washes up to about 500 °C would degas in place before its pores close. What are the failure modes: a CIP bag leak or puncture that lets water or oil into the powder (and the hydrogen that water generates with freshly exposed Al), lubricant decomposition, trapped air expanding on heating, lamination or end-capping cracks from uniaxial pressing?
3. **Process hazards of each route** when handling fine pure Al powder: combustible-dust and ignition risks while filling dies or bags, drawing fine powder into a vacuum line or pump, venting an evacuated die to air, contact with the CIP fluid, stored energy in the high-pressure vessel, and safe practice for each (inert handling, filters, grounding, PPE).
4. **Melt-in and mixing feasibility.** Would a green part from either route (at what density) melt, coalesce and mix into a 6063 melt at 810-840 °C under argon within 2-10 minutes with only induction stirring? Does CIP versus uniaxial pressing versus vacuum hot pressing change coalescence, metal yield, dross or oxide inclusions on remelting? Use evidence from remelting Al powder compacts, chip or swarf briquettes, PM parts and foundry alloying tablets. If alloying powders (Si, Cu, Mg, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, Zr) are blended into the pure Al before pressing: segregation while filling, and exothermic reactions between Al and these powders on heating (for example the self-propagating Al-Ni, Al-Ti, Al-Fe or Al-Zr reactions in pressed compacts, and how compact density affects ignition), and whether these help or hurt safety and dissolution.
5. **A practical recipe for each route** for a 19 mm diameter by 20-60 mm slug: pressure, dwell, evacuation level, drying or degassing temperature and time, lubricant (or none), mould or die material and sizing, expected density, and how to check a part before it goes into the crucible (Archimedes density and open porosity, a weight-loss or gas-release test on heating). What press force, or what CIP vessel size and pressure rating, does this need?
6. **Recommendation:** which route, or neither, would you choose for a university lab making a few such parts per week, and when would each be the wrong choice? Compare briefly with buying cast master alloys or arc-melting a button from the weighed powders.

## Vacuum-Assisted Uniaxial Die Pressing (Route A) versus Cold Isostatic Pressing (Route B) for Producing Aluminium-Powder Green Parts for Ultrasonic Atomizer Remelting

### 1. Pros-and-Cons Comparison

The following table provides a safety-first, criterion-by-criterion comparison of the two consolidation routes and their sub-variants, based on direct aluminium evidence where available and on general powder-metallurgy practice where noted.

| Criterion | Route A — Vacuum uniaxial pressing | Route B — Cold isostatic pressing (CIP) | Preferred |
|---|---|---|---|
| Process safety during pressing | Powder can remain in an evacuable rigid die or inert glovebox, limiting transfers. Hazards include dust entrainment into the vacuum line, electrostatic ignition, pinch loads, and dust release during venting. Reported Al-powder values span MIE <1–13 mJ, MEC 45–170 g/m³, KSt 162–1100 bar·m/s, and Pmax 8–12.9 bar. Use grounded conductive equipment, filtered vacuum lines, and slow inert-gas venting. (reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 6-7, taveau2019metaldustsexplosion pages 1-2, benson2012safetyconsiderationswhen pages 3-5) | Adds high-pressure stored energy and more powder handling. A punctured wet bag can expose Al to water or oil. Water contacting exposed Al can generate hydrogen by 2Al + 3H₂O → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂. Use an evacuated, leak-tested, double-contained bag and an oil rather than water medium where practicable. (reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 6-7, meluch2010warmcompactionof pages 51-58, kim1998effectoffriction pages 1-2) | **A**, if engineered for combustible metal powder. |
| Safety of green part during remelting | Evacuating the loose bed before pressing removes much free pore gas, but high-density pressing can isolate remaining air, water, or lubricant. A lubricant-free, measurably open-pore compact that is slowly heated under dynamic vacuum is preferable to a nearly closed, un-degassed compact. | An evacuated dry bag can remove free gas before densification and CIP avoids weak low-density zones. A leaking wet bag can introduce water or oil; a sealed but non-evacuated bag merely compresses the original gas. | **A by default**; **B only with an evacuated, dry, leak-tested bag**. |
| Green density achievable | Direct Al-alloy evidence: single-action pressing produced about 2.14 g/cm³ at 100 MPa and 2.57 g/cm³ at 500 MPa. That powder contained lubricant, so it is not a pure-Al calibration. Vacuum changes gas inventory more than the pressure–density curve. (selig2012finiteelementsimulation pages 59-67) | Direct Al evidence: initial packing near 48% theoretical density reached 98% at 600 MPa; other pure-Al/Al–Ni work exceeded 95% at sufficiently high pressure. Typical CIP practice is 200–400 MPa. (andasmas2011phenomenologicalstudyof pages 2-4, eksi2007effectofsintering pages 1-2, meluch2010warmcompactionof pages 51-58) | **B** for maximum density, although maximum density before degassing is not the safest target. |
| Density uniformity | Die-wall friction attenuates pressure. Single-action pressing leaves the remote end least dense; double-action pressing moves the minimum toward mid-height. In Cu–Al compacts, raising H/D from 0.7 to 2.12 increased maximum relative-density difference from 0.0851 to 0.1206; application to pure Al is an extrapolation. (wang2018numericalsimulationof pages 16-22, wang2018numericalsimulationof pages 6-9, beck2012onanovel pages 20-26) | Hydrostatic loading and the moving elastomer wall provide much better uniformity. Direct Al–Ni/pure-Al work found that a 1 min pressure dwell produced good homogeneity, whereas immediate decompression produced a dense surface and lower-density core. (andasmas2011phenomenologicalstudyof pages 2-4, andasmas2011phenomenologicalstudyof pages 4-6) | **B**, especially for long slugs with H/D around 2–3. |
| Green strength, edge integrity, and shedding | Good at adequate pressure, but tall slugs are vulnerable to laminations, end-capping, weak central regions, and ejection damage. Rigid tooling gives clean edges. | Usually higher and more uniform handling strength, without rigid-die ejection. Bag wrinkles and rounded edges are possible; slow decompression may be needed to prevent springback cracking. (meluch2010warmcompactionof pages 51-58, meluch2010warmcompactionof pages 45-51) | **B** for handling; **A** for precise edges. |
| Lubricant need and contamination | Die friction encourages lubricant use, but internal wax or stearate adds carbon and gas. For remelting, use no admixed lubricant; if unavoidable, apply the minimum external die-wall film and validate its removal. | Normally needs no internal lubricant because the bag moves with the powder, avoiding wax decomposition and carbon pickup. | **B**. |
| Bag or pressure-fluid contamination | No bag or pressure fluid. Possible contamination comes from die wear, vacuum grease, O-rings, pump backstreaming, or external die lubricant. | Possible elastomer fragments, mould-release residue, oil permeation, or catastrophic fluid ingress. Literature describes rubber, neoprene, or urethane moulds with water, oil, glycerine, or boron oil. (meluch2010warmcompactionof pages 51-58, eksi2007effectofsintering pages 1-2, kim1998effectoffriction pages 1-2) | **A**. |
| Oxide-film disruption | Axial plastic flow and die-wall shear can crack native oxide locally, but do not remove it. | Hydrostatic compression deforms particles but produces less macroscopic shear. It probably fractures oxide at contacts, but direct evidence that ordinary CIP disrupts pure-Al oxide more effectively than die pressing was not found. | **A, slightly**, for cold oxide cracking; the distinction is uncertain. |
| Residual gas and moisture | Direct evacuation of the loose bed removes free interstitial gas. Al powders have shown about 13–25 ppm H, equivalent to approximately 14.7–27.5 cm³ H₂ per 100 g, mainly associated with water on the oxide. Physisorbed water evolves mainly near 100–200°C; hydroxide-related water and H₂ evolve broadly through 200–450°C. Hydrated oxide transforms near 350°C (623 K). (yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 2-4, davis1995degassingandsurface pages 1-2, estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 6-8, estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 5-6) | Evacuating the bag removes free gas but not oxide-bound water. Fluid exposure can add moisture after drying. A non-evacuated bag traps the initial gas inventory. | **A**, unless B uses vacuum-degassed powder and dry evacuated-bag sealing. |
| Dimensional control and 20 mm limit | Best control. A nominal 19 mm rigid die produces a near-final diameter; springback should be calibrated and every slug checked with a go/no-go gauge. | Flexible-tool shrinkage depends on fill density, bag stiffness, closure geometry, and powder flow. Curvature, taper, and wrinkles are possible, and oversize mould dimensions must be established experimentally. (meluch2010warmcompactionof pages 51-58, beck2012onanovel pages 20-26) | **A**. |
| Simplicity and skill | Straightforward if a guarded press exists, although vacuum ports, filters, inert venting, seals, and preferably double-action tooling add complexity. | Wet-bag CIP requires bag filling, evacuation, sealing, vessel loading, pressure cycling, controlled decompression, stripping, and leak inspection. Dry-bag equipment is faster but difficult to justify for a few parts weekly. | **A** in a university laboratory; toll CIP is preferable to buying a unit for trials. |
| Time per part or batch | Filling, evacuation, pressing, decompression, and ejection can take minutes. Several short slugs are easier than one H/D≈3 slug. Separate thermal degassing dominates total time. | Pressure hold may be seconds to 1 min, but bag preparation and vessel cycling dominate; decompression may take several minutes. Several bags can be processed together. (andasmas2011phenomenologicalstudyof pages 2-4, meluch2010warmcompactionof pages 51-58) | **A** for one-offs; **B** for batches. |
| Equipment capital and consumables | Lowest likely capital if a hydraulic press is available. Requires a hardened die, punches, vacuum hardware, filtration, and guarded/inert venting. Rigid tooling has low recurring consumable cost. | A 200–400 MPa vessel, intensifier, interlocked enclosure, inspection program, and disposable bags impose substantial capital and operating cost. Wet-bag tooling is cheaper but labor intensive. No reliable published toll-service price was found. | **A**; use toll CIP for occasional development work. |
| Vacuum sintering or post-press degassing | A lubricant-free compact can be heated under vacuum while pores remain connected, but vacuum sintering alone cannot remove stable Al₂O₃. Degassing near 350°C is supported for hydrated-oxide conversion; higher temperatures risk pore closure and volatile-alloy-element loss. (yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 4-4, carney1990anxrayphotoelectron pages 86-90, carney1990anxrayphotoelectron pages 90-95) | Post-CIP degassing is possible, but very high density can reduce gas pathways. Degassing loose powder before CIP is preferable. | **A**, or pre-degassed evacuated-bag CIP. |
| Vacuum hot pressing extension | Direct Al-composite evidence: about 90%-dense CIP preforms were hot pressed at 550°C, 10⁻⁵ Torr, and 175–245 MPa for 5 h, producing essentially full density. This improves bonding and degassing but is slow and unnecessary for simple remelt feed. (tanga2004purealmatrix pages 2-3, tanga2004purealmatrix pages 3-5) | CIP can provide a uniform preform before vacuum hot pressing, but this is no longer a simple cold-CIP route. | **Neither for routine feedstock**. |
| Overall recommendation | Best practical cold route for a few parts per week: lubricant-free, double-action vacuum die pressing of short slugs after controlled vacuum drying or degassing, targeting adequate strength with retained open porosity rather than maximum density. | Best cold route for density uniformity and low shedding, but only with pre-degassed powder, a dry evacuated double bag, controlled decompression, and rejection after any suspected leak or fluid contact. | **A over B**, but cast master alloy or an arc-melted button remains safer and more reliable than either green compact. |


*Table: Safety-first comparison of vacuum-assisted uniaxial pressing and CIP for producing aluminium-powder slugs for remelting. Direct aluminium evidence is quantified where available, with other conclusions identified through their cited PM analogies.*

### 2. Which Route Produces the Safer Green Part to Melt, and Why

**Adsorbed and chemically bound water.** Gas-atomized aluminium powder carries an amorphous hydrated oxide layer approximately 2–10 nm thick (kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 2-4, kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 1-2). Total hydrogen content is typically 13–25 ppm (by weight), equivalent to approximately 14.7–27.5 cm³ H₂ per 100 g of powder, which is 50–100 times higher than that of a degassed casting (estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 6-8). Nearly all of this hydrogen originates from water that is physically adsorbed or chemically bonded as hydroxides in the surface oxide layer (kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 2-4). Physisorbed water is released broadly around 100–200 °C; water associated with hydroxide decomposition (Al₂O₃·3H₂O → Al₂O₃·H₂O → γ-Al₂O₃) evolves over approximately 150–500 °C, with a major transition near 350 °C (623 K) (estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 5-6, yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 2-4, yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 4-4). Hydrogen from the reaction 2Al + 3H₂O → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂ evolves sharply above approximately 350–400 °C and peaks near 450 °C (725 K for pure Al) (yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 2-4, kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 10-11). The optimum vacuum degassing temperature for Al powder consolidation is identified as 623 K (350 °C); for applications requiring minimal blistering, temperatures above 673 K (400 °C) are recommended (yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 4-4).

**Open-to-closed porosity transition.** As aluminium compacts are pressed above approximately 85–90% relative density, pores begin to disconnect and become closed, trapping whatever gas remains inside (meluch2010warmcompactionof pages 45-51). This is the critical safety threshold: a compact pressed to, say, 95% density without prior degassing can seal in air, adsorbed water, and hydroxide-derived hydrogen. When subsequently heated past 350–450 °C, water reacts with freshly exposed aluminium to generate hydrogen gas in a sealed cavity, potentially building enough pressure to eject molten metal—consistent with the equipment maker's warning.

**Evacuating the die versus evacuating the CIP bag.** Evacuating the die cavity to ≤10 mbar before pressing removes approximately 99% of the equilibrated free interstitial gas (atmospheric pressure to 10 mbar represents a 100-fold reduction). However, evacuation does not remove oxide-bound water, which requires thermal treatment. A CIP bag can also be evacuated before sealing, but a sealed but non-evacuated bag merely compresses the original gas inventory. A wet-bag CIP leak introduces water or oil directly into the powder, potentially exposing freshly cracked aluminium surfaces to water—a severe hydrogen-generation hazard (reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 6-7).

**Degassing during the vacuum/argon-wash cycle.** An open-pore green compact (below roughly 85–90% density) heated slowly through the vacuum and argon washes up to 500 °C would indeed lose most of its physisorbed and hydroxide-bound water before pore closure occurs at the melting point, because the dehydration temperatures (100–500 °C) fall well below the aluminium solidus (660 °C). The interconnected porosity at 80–88% density permits gas transport to external surfaces under dynamic vacuum. This is a significant safety advantage over a nearly fully dense compact that cannot degas in situ.

**Failure modes.** Route A's primary failure modes are: (i) pressing too densely without prior degassing, sealing gas inside; (ii) lamination or end-capping cracks from ejection, creating weak zones that may fragment unpredictably during heating; (iii) lubricant decomposition producing gas and carbon if an admixed lubricant is used; and (iv) re-adsorption of moisture between pressing and crucible loading. Route B adds: (v) CIP bag leak or puncture that admits water or oil to the powder, generating hydrogen on freshly exposed Al surfaces; (vi) residual bag or mould-release material contributing organic contamination; and (vii) high-pressure stored-energy release in the event of vessel failure. For the specific application of remelting, **Route A (vacuum-assisted uniaxial pressing) produces the safer green part**, provided the compact is pressed lubricant-free to a moderate density that retains open porosity, and the powder is pre-degassed or the compact is degassed in the atomizer's vacuum/argon-wash cycle before melting.

### 3. Process Hazards

**Aluminium dust explosion characteristics.** Aluminium powder in the 15–63 µm range is classified in Dust Hazard Class 3 (St3), with reported explosion parameters including: minimum ignition energy (MIE) as low as <1 mJ and typically 3–13 mJ; minimum explosible concentration (MEC) of 45–170 g/m³; deflagration index (K_St) of 162–1100 bar·m/s depending on particle size, shape, and test conditions; and maximum explosion pressure (P_max) of 8–12.9 bar (reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 6-7, taveau2019metaldustsexplosion pages 1-2, benson2012safetyconsiderationswhen pages 3-5, cadwallader2003dustcombustionsafety pages 34-38). Metal dust fires cannot be fought with water, CO₂, or nitrogen; only Class D dry-powder agents, dry sand, or dry sodium chloride should be used (cheremisinoff2014dustexplosionand pages 229-232).

**Route A hazards.** Filling an open die generates airborne dust; drawing fine powder into a vacuum line can deposit it in the pump and downstream piping; venting an evacuated die to air disperses fine dust. Mitigation: fill in a fume hood or glovebox under argon; use sintered-metal filters on the vacuum line with an isolation valve; ground all conductive components; vent slowly with dry argon rather than air; wear appropriate PPE including conductive anti-static clothing, safety glasses, and a P3 dust respirator (benson2012safetyconsiderationswhen pages 2-3, cheremisinoff2014dustexplosionand pages 59-63).

**Route B hazards.** CIP adds high-pressure stored energy (a 25 mm bore × 100 mm long vessel at 300 MPa stores substantial elastic energy in the fluid and vessel), requiring a certified vessel, pressure relief, and barricade or blast containment. Bag filling disperses dust; a punctured bag in a water-based system brings water into contact with freshly cracked aluminium powder, generating hydrogen. Mitigation: use oil-based or boron-oil fluid rather than water; double-bag the powder in a glovebox; leak-test the bag before insertion; operate the CIP behind a blast screen; inspect bags and seals after every cycle (eksi2007effectofsintering pages 1-2, kim1998effectoffriction pages 1-2).

**Safe practices common to both routes:** inert-atmosphere handling (argon glovebox or bag-in/bag-out procedure); electrical grounding of all equipment and the operator; anti-static, conductive flooring; filtered local exhaust ventilation; no compressed-air cleaning; housekeeping to prevent dust accumulation; approved storage in sealed conductive containers away from ignition sources (benson2012safetyconsiderationswhen pages 2-3, cheremisinoff2014dustexplosionand pages 59-63).

### 4. Melt-In and Mixing Feasibility

**Remelting evidence.** No study was found that directly reports remelting a pressed pure-aluminium-powder compact into an aluminium melt under the specific conditions described. However, closely analogous evidence exists from aluminium chip/swarf briquettes. Cold-pressed Al–Si–Mg chip briquettes (density 2.29 g/cm³, 12.1% porosity) remelted in an induction furnace at approximately 850 °C achieved a metallurgical yield of 94.2%, with only 2.25% dross, and the resulting casting was chemically homogeneous with no significant segregation (baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 18-20, baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 16-18, baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 20-21). Puga et al. (2009) found that Al swarf briquettes incorporated at 81–85% under argon at 850 °C, with induction melting outperforming resistance melting (83–85% vs 63–69% incorporation), and dross at 10–14% under argon versus 27–35% without protection (puga2009recyclingofaluminium pages 4-5). Higher melting temperatures (up to 950 °C) slightly improved incorporation and reduced melting time from 65 to 50 minutes for their charge sizes.

**Applicability to pressed powder compacts.** A pressed powder compact differs from a chip briquette in having a much higher specific oxide area (each 15–63 µm particle is individually oxide-coated), but the oxide thickness is only 2–10 nm (kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 2-4), much thinner than the heavily oxidised machining chips. In the user's crucible at 810–840 °C under argon with induction stirring, a 10–40 g compact submerged in a 170–350 g melt should heat through its 19 mm cross-section within approximately 1–2 minutes and melt within the 2–10 minute hold. The induction field provides electromagnetic stirring that, while not mechanical, promotes convective mixing. A compact at 85–90% density with open porosity will fragment as aluminium melts and wets inward, liberating individual oxide skins as fine γ-Al₂O₃ particles that should float to the surface as dross. By analogy with briquette remelting, metal yield of approximately 90–95% is a reasonable expectation for a pre-degassed, lubricant-free compact under argon, with the principal loss being oxide-skin dross (extrapolated from chip-briquette data). Achieving yield at the higher end of this range requires minimising re-oxidation during loading and melting.

**CIP versus uniaxial versus vacuum hot pressing.** The consolidation method primarily affects remelting through its influence on residual gas and porosity distribution. A uniformly porous CIP compact and a uniaxially pressed compact with some density gradient should both melt and coalesce, but the CIP compact may break up more uniformly. A vacuum-hot-pressed compact approaching full density would melt in the same manner as a solid piece of aluminium—no gas ejection risk—but vacuum hot pressing at 550 °C and 175–245 MPa for hours is disproportionate effort for a simple remelt feedstock (tanga2004purealmatrix pages 2-3, tanga2004purealmatrix pages 3-5).

**Alloying-powder blends: segregation and exothermic reactions.** If Si, Cu, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, or Zr powders are blended into the Al before pressing, segregation during die filling (density- and size-driven) must be controlled by careful blending and incremental filling. More critically, binary Al–Ni compacts can undergo self-propagating high-temperature synthesis (SHS) with ignition near 640 °C for Ni+Al→Ni₃Al, well below the atomizer melt temperature of 810–840 °C (morsi2026reviewcombustionsynthesis pages 6-7). Al–Ti compacts have a lower exothermicity (adiabatic temperature ~1518 K for TiAl) and may not self-sustain without preheating, but the onset of solid-state reaction is composition- and density-dependent (adeli2016theselfpropagatinghigh pages 1-3, adeli2016theselfpropagatinghigh pages 3-6). The optimal compact green density for SHS is approximately 60–70% of theoretical; higher density improves particle contact and can raise combustion temperature (adeli2016theselfpropagatinghigh pages 3-6, morsi2026reviewcombustionsynthesis pages 6-7). Moisture in compacts promotes porosity and can slow or disrupt the combustion wave (morsi2026reviewcombustionsynthesis pages 9-10). For the user's application, SHS reactions are a potential safety hazard during the slow heating ramp: if the compact reaches the ignition temperature before being submerged in the melt, a runaway exotherm could eject material. **Use of Ni, Ti, Fe, or Zr elemental powders blended with Al in a pressed compact is therefore strongly discouraged for this application.** Master-alloy powders or pre-alloyed powders, where the elements are already in solid solution or as stable intermetallics, do not support SHS and are safer.

### 5. Practical Recipes

The following table provides starting recipes for each route, with specific pressures, forces, evacuation levels, and quality checks.

| Parameter | Route A — Vacuum uniaxial die pressing | Route B — Vacuum-degassed, evacuated-bag CIP |
|---|---|---|
| Powder preparation | Use clean gas-atomized Al and sieve gently without creating a dust cloud. Blend additions in a sealed conductive container by low-energy tumbling. Prefer two or three 20–30 mm slugs rather than one 60 mm slug to limit die-friction gradients. | Use the same powder preparation. Fill the mould incrementally with gentle vibration. Validate blending and filling because powders of different size or density can segregate. |
| Drying / degassing | Minimum: dynamic vacuum at 100–150°C for 2–4 h. Preferred qualified treatment: loose powder near 350°C (623 K) for 2–5 h, followed by cooling and transfer without air exposure. Physisorbed water evolves mainly at 100–200°C; hydroxide-related water and H₂ continue through roughly 200–450°C. (yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 2-4, davis1995degassingandsurface pages 1-2, yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 4-4, estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 5-6, kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 10-11) | Degas loose powder before bagging with the same qualified schedule. Cool under vacuum or dry Ar, transfer in a glovebox, then evacuate and seal the bag. Reject powder after suspected water or oil contact. |
| Pressing pressure | Start at 200–300 MPa; qualify higher pressure only if handling strength is inadequate. Use double-action pressing for tall slugs or divide them into shorter pieces. *Table: Safety-first starting recipes for producing 19 mm diameter aluminium-powder slugs by vacuum die pressing or evacuated-bag CIP. Values requiring qualification on the actual powder and equipment are presented as development ranges rather than validated production limits.*

### 6. Recommendation

For a university laboratory making a few 19 mm × 20–60 mm aluminium-powder slugs per week for remelting in an ultrasonic atomizer:

**Route A (vacuum-assisted uniaxial die pressing) is recommended over Route B (CIP).** Route A is simpler, requires less capital (a guarded hydraulic press, hardened die, and vacuum hardware versus a certified high-pressure CIP vessel and ancillaries), introduces no fluid-contact failure mode, and provides better dimensional control for the tight 19 mm clearance. With lubricant-free pressing at 200–300 MPa after vacuum drying of the powder, targeting 85–90% theoretical density with retained open porosity, the compact can degas in situ during the atomizer's vacuum and argon-wash cycles before its pores close at the melting point. The compact should be pressed as short slugs (H/D ≤ 1.5, i.e. ≤ 28 mm long) using double-action punches to minimise density gradients (wang2018numericalsimulationof pages 16-22, beck2012onanovel pages 20-26). Every slug should be verified by Archimedes density and a go/no-go gauge before loading.

**When Route A is the wrong choice:** (i) if a tall slug (H/D > 2) is required and density uniformity is critical—CIP is then better for structural uniformity, but use pre-degassed powder in a dry evacuated bag; (ii) if the laboratory already has access to a CIP facility or toll-pressing service and not a suitable press, sending occasional parts out for CIP may be faster than building tooling in-house.

**When Route B is the wrong choice:** (i) if no CIP facility is available and the cost of a vessel is not justified for a few parts per week; (ii) if only water-based CIP fluid is available, because any bag leak exposes Al powder to water; (iii) if the operator cannot reliably verify bag integrity and vacuum seal before and after pressing.

**When neither route is the best choice:** Cast master alloys or an arc-melted button from the weighed elemental charges remain safer and more reliable than any green pressed compact. A fully pre-melted and solidified charge piece contains no trapped gas, no adsorbed water, no individual particle oxide shells, and no risk of powder ejection—it simply remelts. The trade-off is that arc melting requires an arc furnace and produces only one composition per melt, while pressing is a room-temperature process that can incorporate custom powder blends. For standard alloy compositions (6063, 4047) where commercial master alloys are available, the recommendation is to **prefer cast or arc-melted charge pieces over either pressed-powder route**, and to reserve powder pressing for compositions where no suitable master alloy exists and where the added risks can be justified and managed.

### Evidence Basis and Limitations

Direct aluminium-specific evidence is available for: green density versus pressure in CIP (eksi2007effectofsintering pages 1-2, andasmas2011phenomenologicalstudyof pages 2-4); degassing temperatures and hydrogen content of gas-atomised Al powder (yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 2-4, yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 4-4, estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 6-8, kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 2-4, estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 5-6, kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 7-8); Al-powder explosion parameters (reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 6-7, taveau2019metaldustsexplosion pages 1-2, benson2012safetyconsiderationswhen pages 3-5); SHS ignition in Al–Ni and Al–Ti compacts (morsi2026reviewcombustionsynthesis pages 6-7, adeli2016theselfpropagatinghigh pages 3-6); vacuum hot pressing of Al composites (tanga2004purealmatrix pages 2-3, tanga2004purealmatrix pages 3-5); and remelting of Al chip briquettes (puga2009recyclingofaluminium pages 4-5, baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 18-20, baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 16-18). Density-gradient data for uniaxially pressed compacts at various H/D ratios are extrapolated from Cu–Al mixed-powder simulations (wang2018numericalsimulationof pages 16-22, wang2018numericalsimulationof pages 6-9); general CIP descriptions are from PM textbook-level sources applied to aluminium (meluch2010warmcompactionof pages 51-58, beck2012onanovel pages 20-26); and the specific behavior of a pressed Al-powder green compact during remelting in a small induction-heated crucible has not been directly studied in the published literature and is inferred from briquette remelting studies and PM degassing work. The oxide-disruption mechanism in CIP versus uniaxial pressing for pure aluminium powder has not been experimentally compared in any study identified in this review; the conclusion that uniaxial pressing introduces slightly more shear-induced oxide cracking is a reasonable inference from general PM principles but is not validated for this system.

The following table provides a safety-first, criterion-by-criterion comparison of the two consolidation routes and their sub-variants, based on direct aluminium evidence where available and on general powder-metallurgy practice where noted.

| Criterion | Route A — Vacuum uniaxial pressing | Route B — Cold isostatic pressing (CIP) | Preferred |
|---|---|---|---|
| Process safety during pressing | Powder can remain in an evacuable rigid die or inert glovebox, limiting transfers. Hazards include dust entrainment into the vacuum line, electrostatic ignition, pinch loads, and dust release during venting. Reported Al-powder values span MIE <1–13 mJ, MEC 45–170 g/m³, KSt 162–1100 bar·m/s, and Pmax 8–12.9 bar. Use grounded conductive equipment, filtered vacuum lines, and slow inert-gas venting. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029) | Adds high-pressure stored energy and more powder handling. A punctured wet bag can expose Al to water or oil. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000057) | **A**, if engineered for combustible metal powder. |

(pqac-00000053) | Direct Al evidence: initial packing near 48% theoretical density reached 98% at 600 MPa; other pure-Al/Al–Ni work exceeded 95% at sufficiently high pressure. ### 2. Which Route Produces the Safer Green Part to Melt, and Why

**Adsorbed and chemically bound water.** Gas-atomized aluminium powder carries an amorphous hydrated oxide layer approximately 2–10 nm thick (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000072). Total hydrogen content is typically 13–25 ppm (by weight), equivalent to approximately 14.7–27.5 cm³ H₂ per 100 g of powder, which is 50–100 times higher than that of a degassed casting (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000011). Nearly all of this hydrogen originates from water that is physically adsorbed or chemically bonded as hydroxides in the surface oxide layer (pqac-00000066). Physisorbed water is released broadly around 100–200 °C; water associated with hydroxide decomposition (Al₂O₃·3H₂O → Al₂O₃·H₂O → γ-Al₂O₃) evolves over approximately 150–500 °C, with a major transition near 350 °C (623 K) (pqac-00000067, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000010). Hydrogen from the reaction 2Al + 3H₂O → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂ evolves sharply above approximately 350–400 °C and peaks near 450 °C (725 K for pure Al) (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000070). The optimum vacuum degassing temperature for Al powder consolidation is identified as 623 K (350 °C); for applications requiring minimal blistering, temperatures above 673 K (400 °C) are recommended (pqac-00000010).

**Open-to-closed porosity transition.** As aluminium compacts are pressed above approximately 85–90% relative density, pores begin to disconnect and become closed, trapping whatever gas remains inside (pqac-00000058). This is the critical safety threshold: a compact pressed to, say, 95% density without prior degassing can seal in air, adsorbed water, and hydroxide-derived hydrogen. When subsequently heated past 350–450 °C, water reacts with freshly exposed aluminium to generate hydrogen gas in a sealed cavity, potentially building enough pressure to eject molten metal—consistent with the equipment maker's warning.

**Evacuating the die versus evacuating the CIP bag.** Evacuating the die cavity to ≤10 mbar before pressing removes approximately 99% of the equilibrated free interstitial gas (atmospheric pressure to 10 mbar represents a 100-fold reduction). However, evacuation does not remove oxide-bound water, which requires thermal treatment. A CIP bag can also be evacuated before sealing, but a sealed but non-evacuated bag merely compresses the original gas inventory. A wet-bag CIP leak introduces water or oil directly into the powder, potentially exposing freshly cracked aluminium surfaces to water—a severe hydrogen-generation hazard (pqac-00000022).

**Degassing during the vacuum/argon-wash cycle.** An open-pore green compact (below roughly 85–90% density) heated slowly through the vacuum and argon washes up to 500 °C would indeed lose most of its physisorbed and hydroxide-bound water before pore closure occurs at the melting point, because the dehydration temperatures (100–500 °C) fall well below the aluminium solidus (660 °C). The interconnected porosity at 80–88% density permits gas transport to external surfaces under dynamic vacuum. This is a significant safety advantage over a nearly fully dense compact that cannot degas in situ.

**Failure modes.** Route A's primary failure modes are: (i) pressing too densely without prior degassing, sealing gas inside; (ii) lamination or end-capping cracks from ejection, creating weak zones that may fragment unpredictably during heating; (iii) lubricant decomposition producing gas and carbon if an admixed lubricant is used; and (iv) re-adsorption of moisture between pressing and crucible loading. Route B adds: (v) CIP bag leak or puncture that admits water or oil to the powder, generating hydrogen on freshly exposed Al surfaces; (vi) residual bag or mould-release material contributing organic contamination; and (vii) high-pressure stored-energy release in the event of vessel failure. For the specific application of remelting, **Route A (vacuum-assisted uniaxial pressing) produces the safer green part**, provided the compact is pressed lubricant-free to a moderate density that retains open porosity, and the powder is pre-degassed or the compact is degassed in the atomizer's vacuum/argon-wash cycle before melting.

### 3. Process Hazards

**Aluminium dust explosion characteristics.** Aluminium powder in the 15–63 µm range is classified in Dust Hazard Class 3 (St3), with reported explosion parameters including: minimum ignition energy (MIE) as low as <1 mJ and typically 3–13 mJ; minimum explosible concentration (MEC) of 45–170 g/m³; deflagration index (K_St) of 162–1100 bar·m/s depending on particle size, shape, and test conditions; and maximum explosion pressure (P_max) of 8–12.9 bar (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000027). Metal dust fires cannot be fought with water, CO₂, or nitrogen; only Class D dry-powder agents, dry sand, or dry sodium chloride should be used (pqac-00000026).

**Route A hazards.** Filling an open die generates airborne dust; drawing fine powder into a vacuum line can deposit it in the pump and downstream piping; venting an evacuated die to air disperses fine dust. Mitigation: fill in a fume hood or glovebox under argon; use sintered-metal filters on the vacuum line with an isolation valve; ground all conductive components; vent slowly with dry argon rather than air; wear appropriate PPE including conductive anti-static clothing, safety glasses, and a P3 dust respirator (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000024).

**Route B hazards.** CIP adds high-pressure stored energy (a 25 mm bore × 100 mm long vessel at 300 MPa stores substantial elastic energy in the fluid and vessel), requiring a certified vessel, pressure relief, and barricade or blast containment. Bag filling disperses dust; a punctured bag in a water-based system brings water into contact with freshly cracked aluminium powder, generating hydrogen. Mitigation: use oil-based or boron-oil fluid rather than water; double-bag the powder in a glovebox; leak-test the bag before insertion; operate the CIP behind a blast screen; inspect bags and seals after every cycle (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000057).

**Safe practices common to both routes:** inert-atmosphere handling (argon glovebox or bag-in/bag-out procedure); electrical grounding of all equipment and the operator; anti-static, conductive flooring; filtered local exhaust ventilation; no compressed-air cleaning; housekeeping to prevent dust accumulation; approved storage in sealed conductive containers away from ignition sources (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000024).

### 4. Melt-In and Mixing Feasibility

**Remelting evidence.** No study was found that directly reports remelting a pressed pure-aluminium-powder compact into an aluminium melt under the specific conditions described. However, closely analogous evidence exists from aluminium chip/swarf briquettes. Cold-pressed Al–Si–Mg chip briquettes (density 2.29 g/cm³, 12.1% porosity) remelted in an induction furnace at approximately 850 °C achieved a metallurgical yield of 94.2%, with only 2.25% dross, and the resulting casting was chemically homogeneous with no significant segregation (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017). Puga et al. (2009) found that Al swarf briquettes incorporated at 81–85% under argon at 850 °C, with induction melting outperforming resistance melting (83–85% vs 63–69% incorporation), and dross at 10–14% under argon versus 27–35% without protection (pqac-00000014). Higher melting temperatures (up to 950 °C) slightly improved incorporation and reduced melting time from 65 to 50 minutes for their charge sizes.

**Applicability to pressed powder compacts.** A pressed powder compact differs from a chip briquette in having a much higher specific oxide area (each 15–63 µm particle is individually oxide-coated), but the oxide thickness is only 2–10 nm (pqac-00000066), much thinner than the heavily oxidised machining chips. In the user's crucible at 810–840 °C under argon with induction stirring, a 10–40 g compact submerged in a 170–350 g melt should heat through its 19 mm cross-section within approximately 1–2 minutes and melt within the 2–10 minute hold. The induction field provides electromagnetic stirring that, while not mechanical, promotes convective mixing. A compact at 85–90% density with open porosity will fragment as aluminium melts and wets inward, liberating individual oxide skins as fine γ-Al₂O₃ particles that should float to the surface as dross. By analogy with briquette remelting, metal yield of approximately 90–95% is a reasonable expectation for a pre-degassed, lubricant-free compact under argon, with the principal loss being oxide-skin dross (extrapolated from chip-briquette data). Achieving yield at the higher end of this range requires minimising re-oxidation during loading and melting.

**CIP versus uniaxial versus vacuum hot pressing.** The consolidation method primarily affects remelting through its influence on residual gas and porosity distribution. A uniformly porous CIP compact and a uniaxially pressed compact with some density gradient should both melt and coalesce, but the CIP compact may break up more uniformly. A vacuum-hot-pressed compact approaching full density would melt in the same manner as a solid piece of aluminium—no gas ejection risk—but vacuum hot pressing at 550 °C and 175–245 MPa for hours is disproportionate effort for a simple remelt feedstock (pqac-00000064, pqac-00000065).

**Alloying-powder blends: segregation and exothermic reactions.** If Si, Cu, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, or Zr powders are blended into the Al before pressing, segregation during die filling (density- and size-driven) must be controlled by careful blending and incremental filling. More critically, binary Al–Ni compacts can undergo self-propagating high-temperature synthesis (SHS) with ignition near 640 °C for Ni+Al→Ni₃Al, well below the atomizer melt temperature of 810–840 °C (pqac-00000033). Al–Ti compacts have a lower exothermicity (adiabatic temperature ~1518 K for TiAl) and may not self-sustain without preheating, but the onset of solid-state reaction is composition- and density-dependent (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). The optimal compact green density for SHS is approximately 60–70% of theoretical; higher density improves particle contact and can raise combustion temperature (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033). Moisture in compacts promotes porosity and can slow or disrupt the combustion wave (pqac-00000037). For the user's application, SHS reactions are a potential safety hazard during the slow heating ramp: if the compact reaches the ignition temperature before being submerged in the melt, a runaway exotherm could eject material. **Use of Ni, Ti, Fe, or Zr elemental powders blended with Al in a pressed compact is therefore strongly discouraged for this application.** Master-alloy powders or pre-alloyed powders, where the elements are already in solid solution or as stable intermetallics, do not support SHS and are safer.

### 6. Recommendation

For a university laboratory making a few 19 mm × 20–60 mm aluminium-powder slugs per week for remelting in an ultrasonic atomizer:

**Route A (vacuum-assisted uniaxial die pressing) is recommended over Route B (CIP).** Route A is simpler, requires less capital (a guarded hydraulic press, hardened die, and vacuum hardware versus a certified high-pressure CIP vessel and ancillaries), introduces no fluid-contact failure mode, and provides better dimensional control for the tight 19 mm clearance. With lubricant-free pressing at 200–300 MPa after vacuum drying of the powder, targeting 85–90% theoretical density with retained open porosity, the compact can degas in situ during the atomizer's vacuum and argon-wash cycles before its pores close at the melting point. The compact should be pressed as short slugs (H/D ≤ 1.5, i.e. ≤ 28 mm long) using double-action punches to minimise density gradients (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000052). Every slug should be verified by Archimedes density and a go/no-go gauge before loading.

**When Route A is the wrong choice:** (i) if a tall slug (H/D > 2) is required and density uniformity is critical—CIP is then better for structural uniformity, but use pre-degassed powder in a dry evacuated bag; (ii) if the laboratory already has access to a CIP facility or toll-pressing service and not a suitable press, sending occasional parts out for CIP may be faster than building tooling in-house.

**When Route B is the wrong choice:** (i) if no CIP facility is available and the cost of a vessel is not justified for a few parts per week; (ii) if only water-based CIP fluid is available, because any bag leak exposes Al powder to water; (iii) if the operator cannot reliably verify bag integrity and vacuum seal before and after pressing.

**When neither route is the best choice:** Cast master alloys or an arc-melted button from the weighed elemental charges remain safer and more reliable than any green pressed compact. A fully pre-melted and solidified charge piece contains no trapped gas, no adsorbed water, no individual particle oxide shells, and no risk of powder ejection—it simply remelts. The trade-off is that arc melting requires an arc furnace and produces only one composition per melt, while pressing is a room-temperature process that can incorporate custom powder blends. For standard alloy compositions (6063, 4047) where commercial master alloys are available, the recommendation is to **prefer cast or arc-melted charge pieces over either pressed-powder route**, and to reserve powder pressing for compositions where no suitable master alloy exists and where the added risks can be justified and managed.

### Evidence Basis and Limitations

Direct aluminium-specific evidence is available for: green density versus pressure in CIP (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000001); degassing temperatures and hydrogen content of gas-atomised Al powder (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000066, pqac-00000067, pqac-00000068, pqac-00000069); Al-powder explosion parameters (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029); SHS ignition in Al–Ni and Al–Ti compacts (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000032); vacuum hot pressing of Al composites (pqac-00000064, pqac-00000065); and remelting of Al chip briquettes (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). Density-gradient data for uniaxially pressed compacts at various H/D ratios are extrapolated from Cu–Al mixed-powder simulations (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000048); general CIP descriptions are from PM textbook-level sources applied to aluminium (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000056); and the specific behavior of a pressed Al-powder green compact during remelting in a small induction-heated crucible has not been directly studied in the published literature and is inferred from briquette remelting studies and PM degassing work. The oxide-disruption mechanism in CIP versus uniaxial pressing for pure aluminium powder has not been experimentally compared in any study identified in this review; the conclusion that uniaxial pressing introduces slightly more shear-induced oxide cracking is a reasonable inference from general PM principles but is not validated for this system.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides only a qualitative comparison and does not report the requested numerical green densities for aluminum powder at pressures from 100 to 600 MPa. It states that cold isostatic pressing (CIP) applies compaction pressure through a pressurized fluid, with the powder held in a flexible mold. CIP produces a highly uniform density distribution, implying minimal density gradients throughout the compact, but it is slow and gives poor dimensional tolerances. Uniaxial die compaction places powder in a rigid die and applies pressure through punches, either from one direction (single action) or from both top and bottom (double action). Die-wall friction reduces the transmitted pressure along the compact, creating density gradients. In single-action pressing, the bottom has the lowest pressure and density; in double-action pressing, pressure is minimized near the center, known as the density split. Thus, the excerpt supports the conclusion that CIP is more uniform, while uniaxial pressing has greater density variation, but specific pressure-density values and a quantitative comparison for aluminum are absent from these pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that cold isostatic pressing (CIP) of pure aluminum produces substantial densification, exceeding 95% of the theoretical density. It does not provide the specific green-density values at each pressure between 100 and 600 MPa, nor does it include a direct comparison with uniaxial die pressing. Regarding uniformity, the authors state that holding the sample at the pressure plateau for one minute was used to ensure good density homogeneity throughout the compact. In preliminary experiments where samples were depressurized immediately, a significant density gradient developed: the surface had higher density while the core had lower density. Thus, CIP can achieve high density and relatively uniform compacts when an adequate pressure-holding period is applied, whereas insufficient equilibration produces a surface-to-core density gradient. The supplied pages do not establish the corresponding density uniformity or gradient for uniaxial die pressing.
contexts.question: What green density does cold isostatic pressing of aluminum powder achieve at different pressures (100-600 MPa), and how does it compare to uniaxial die pressing? What is the density uniformity and density gradient in each?

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide data for cold isostatic pressing (CIP) of aluminum powder over 100–600 MPa, so it cannot establish CIP green densities, uniformity, or gradients across that pressure range. It does provide a comparison for uniaxial die compaction of internal-structure compacts and conventional powder-metallurgy compacts, primarily from 100 to 400 MPa. Internal-structure compacts have similar powder densification to conventional compacts but lower overall bulk density because the internal structure is less dense than the powder compact. At 100 MPa, the internal-structure compact exhibits sharper and more pronounced density gradients, including a high-density band around the internal structure and low-density regions near the top and bottom; the conventional compact is more uniformly densified. At 200 MPa, the internal-structure compact’s measured relative-density range is 84–96%, compared with an approximately three-times larger range at 100 MPa (65–95%), indicating improved uniformity with increasing pressure. The excerpt also reports that internal structures can produce localized densification exceeding that of conventional compacts at equal pressure, potentially enabling comparable densification at lower pressing pressures.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports thermal-transition temperatures but does not provide quantitative moisture content, adsorbed-water content, or hydrogen-gas content in mass percent or mL H2 per gram. It states that hydrated Al2O3 decomposes to crystalline Al2O3 at 623 K in vacuum. The associated oxidation reaction involving water of hydration occurs at 623 K, whereas desorption of chemisorbed hydrogen occurs around 725 K. Thus, the excerpt distinguishes hydrated-water-related oxide decomposition at 623 K from later hydrogen desorption at approximately 725 K. It also notes that gas-atomized aluminum powder has ultramicropores and that H2O adsorbed inside these pores desorbs differently from water on the outer surface, but no specific desorption temperature for either adsorbed-water population is given here. For processing, 623 K is identified as the optimum degassing temperature for powder consolidation; temperatures above 673 K are recommended for high-temperature applications to reduce blistering caused by subsequent H2 desorption. The excerpt refers to chemisorbed hydrogen rather than explicitly identifying a separate chemisorbed-water decomposition temperature.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide quantitative moisture content, total adsorbed-water loading, or hydrogen gas content in mass percent or mL H2 per gram. It reports only a BET surface area based on water adsorption, ABET(H2O) = 0.125 m² g−1. For humid-air-exposed powder, water desorption begins around 480 K and peaks near 720 K. The authors identify three water populations: water adsorbed on the outer surface, water adsorbed on pore walls, and water chemically bound as hydration water in hydrated aluminum oxide. Water retained in ultramicropores may require high-temperature outgassing. The cited dehydration/decomposition pathways span approximately 423–448 K for Al2O3·3H2O to Al2O3·2.5H2O, 583–773 K for the next dehydration step, and 773–823 K for conversion to α-Al2O3; hydroxide decomposition occurs at 353–500 K for Al(OH)3 → AlOOH and 573–750 K for AlOOH → α-Al2O3. XPS indicates amorphous hydrated alumina transforms to crystalline alumina at about 623 K. Hydrogen evolution is delayed until roughly 620 K, increases sharply around 620–660 K, and peaks near 725 K. The authors distinguish alumina transformation at 623 K from chemisorbed-hydrogen desorption at 725 K.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence for remelting a cold-pressed aluminum-chip briquette, but not for pressed aluminum powder or powder-metallurgy (PM) compacts specifically. Sample A was melted in an induction furnace at approximately 850 °C and then unidirectionally solidified into Sample B. Remelting converted the mechanically porous chip compact into a substantially more coherent metallic casting: density increased from 2.29 to 2.388 g·cm⁻³, while porosity decreased from 12.1% to 8.15%. The text attributes this to elimination of gaps between chips and transformation into a compact metallic volume, although residual porosity remained from dissolved hydrogen, oxidation, and decomposition of entrapped oils or emulsions. The reported output mass was 273.41 g from a 290.25 g briquette input. The metallurgical metal yield was approximately 94.20%, with a reported dross/oxide-residue fraction of approximately 2.25% and total calculated weight loss of 10.3 g. The resulting casting was described as homogeneous, with stable composition and predictable behavior. No melting time, rate of coalescence, or direct observations of floating, sinking, breakup, or incorporation kinetics are reported in this excerpt. It also does not establish performance for pressed aluminum powder compacts.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides indirect evidence about remelting cold-pressed aluminum-chip briquettes, but it does not report detailed experimental measurements of melting time, coalescence, or dross mass. The briquettes were made from AlSi- and AlMgSi-alloy machining chips, mechanically cleaned, centrifuged to remove lubricants and coolant, magnetically separated to remove ferromagnetic contaminants, and cold pressed without binders at 100–160 MPa. Their high density and low porosity are presented as important for remelting behavior: compaction is expected to reduce oxidation during heating, limit metal loss as fine particulate matter, stabilize composition, and improve aluminum recovery. The excerpt cites an expected aluminum yield of 80–90%, depending on the melting method, but this is a general value rather than a clearly reported result from the described remelting experiment. Cleaning is specifically intended to reduce dross formation and oxide inclusions by removing oils and steel particles. One briquette was remelted in an induction furnace at approximately 850 °C and cast into a mold for subsequent homogeneity analysis. No evidence is provided here for remelting pressed aluminum powder compacts or conventional powder-metallurgy (PM) compacts, and no direct observations of briquette sinking, breakup, dissolution, coalescence, or residence/melting time are included in pages 5–7.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports remelting behavior for cold-pressed recycled aluminum chip briquettes, although it does not specifically document pressed aluminum powder or powder-metallurgy (PM) compacts, nor does it report melting time. The pressed briquette initially had pronounced intergranular porosity, residual oils, and a heterogeneous surface, with a density of 2.29 g/cm³ and porosity of 12.1%. Following melting and resolidification, the material became more compact: density rose to 2.388 g/cm³ and porosity fell to 8.15%. The authors attribute this primarily to elimination of mechanical voids between chips during melting, while residual gas-related porosity remained because of oil decomposition. These observations provide evidence of coalescence/ consolidation during remelting, but not a detailed description of the kinetics or extent of individual briquette breakup and liquid-metal coalescence. The remelted material showed compositional homogeneity, no significant alloy segregation, and only thin residual oxidation layers. Metallurgical recovery was 94.2%, while dross represented 2.25%, indicating effective recovery and limited oxidation loss under the reported conditions. The study concludes that properly processed briquettes have predictable melting behavior and are viable secondary aluminum additives, while emphasizing oil removal, oxidation reduction, and higher pressing density as ways to reduce porosity and improve remelting performance.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence for remelting compacted aluminum machining swarf briquettes, but not for pressed aluminum powder compacts or powder-metallurgy (PM) compacts specifically. Briquetting is described as beneficial because compacted swarf melts inside the molten pool, avoiding the poor behavior expected from loose, high-volume-to-weight chips. Under a protected argon atmosphere at 850 °C, metal incorporation from briquettes was approximately 81.3–85.4%, compared with 58.7–62.0% without protection. Dross was approximately 11.7–13.5% of briquette mass under argon, versus 32.5–34.8% without protection. Furnace type also mattered: induction melting gave about 83.3–85.1% incorporation and 9.6–11.4% dross, whereas resistance melting gave 62.5–68.8% incorporation and 27.1–32.3% dross under the reported conditions. At 800 °C, incorporation was 79.5–81.8% with 14.1–15.5% dross; at 900 °C it was 82.6–84.8% with 11.7–12.7% dross; and at 950 °C it was 82.2–85.2% with 11.6–13.4% dross. Melting time decreased from 65 minutes at 800 °C to 55 minutes at 900 °C and 50 minutes at 950 °C. The excerpt does not report direct observations or measurements of briquette coalescence, nor does it establish behavior of pressed aluminum powder/PM compacts.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence for remelting cold-pressed aluminum chip/swarf briquettes, but it does not report a quantitative metal recovery or yield, melting time, dross mass, or direct coalescence measurement. Sample A had a bulk density of approximately 2.29 g/cm³, about 12.1% porosity, and 87.9% compaction, with a heterogeneous lamellar structure containing pores, microcracks, oxide fragments, and flattened chip segments. These characteristics are expected to influence remelting: the high specific surface area should promote faster wetting and fragmentation, potentially improving deoxidation kinetics. Conversely, the porous, low-density briquette may remain at the melt surface longer, increasing exposure to oxidation or burn-off and potentially increasing dross formation. The excerpt therefore supports a qualitative tradeoff between rapid breakup/wetting and increased oxidation losses. For Sample B, remelting and resolidification produced a chemically homogeneous casting. Aluminum remained above 97 wt.%, while Mg, Si, Mn, Fe, and Cr were present at low concentrations with no significant spatial deviations. This is evidence that the material can coalesce into a compositionally uniform remelted product, but the supplied pages contain no direct evidence for pressed aluminum powder or conventional PM compacts, nor numerical recovery, yield, melting-duration, or coalescence-rate data.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence for remelting cold-pressed aluminum chip/swarf briquettes, particularly Sample B, but not for pressed aluminum powder compacts or conventional PM compacts. During remelting, mechanical voids are largely eliminated and the material becomes more compact, although residual metallurgical porosity remains because of dissolved hydrogen, oxidation, entrapped gases, and decomposition of oils or cutting emulsions. Sample B achieved a density of 2.388 g·cm⁻³ after melting and exhibited a 2.25% dross fraction, 3.55% relative melting loss, and 94.2% metallurgical yield. Oxide films on the chips separate into the dross rather than entering the metallic matrix; oxygen levels of 3.8–5.9 wt.% were measured by SEM–EDS. Organic contamination lowers briquette density, releases gas during heating, promotes gas porosity, increases burn-off, and reduces yield. The remelted metal becomes chemically homogeneous, with aluminum at 97.21–97.51 wt.% and no significant sampled segregation. Briquettes in the 2.20–2.40 g·cm⁻³ range are described as favorable for steel deoxidation because they fragment rapidly, submerge appropriately, expose reactive surface area, and yield 90–96%. The excerpt gives no quantitative melting-time data and does not directly describe liquid-phase coalescence behavior; it only indicates densification, oxide/dross separation, and homogenization during remelting.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies aluminum powder as an extremely reactive metal dust with severe explosion characteristics. It reports a minimum ignition energy below 10 mJ, indicating high sensitivity to ignition sources. Aluminum is classified as St3, and the text gives KSt values above 300 bar·m/s and maximum explosion pressures above 10 bar. Table 1 lists representative aluminum values of KSt = 515 bar·m/s and Pmax = 11.2 bar; however, the article also notes that measured severity depends on particle size, oxide film, test apparatus, and vessel volume. In particular, Table 2 reports aluminum at KSt = 162 bar·m/s and Pmax = 8.0 bar in a 20-L sphere, versus KSt = 328 bar·m/s and Pmax = 10.1 bar in a 1-m³ chamber. The larger-scale increase may result from stronger thermal radiation and can cause conventional testing to underestimate risk. The excerpt does not provide a minimum explosible concentration (MEC), nor does it detail specific handling controls such as grounding, inerting procedures, PPE, or the reaction of aluminum powder with water producing hydrogen. It does caution that highly reactive metal powders may burn in carbon dioxide, water vapor, and nitrogen, and that explosion protection should supplement preventive measures.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides information primarily on SHS of Ni–Al, especially Ni3Al, rather than Al–Ti. The reaction mechanism involves melting aluminum, its spreading and wetting of nickel, followed by an exothermic reaction that generates heat and sustains combustion; it is characterized as reactive transient liquid-phase sintering. Particle size strongly affects ignition and combustion. Large nickel particles can cause incomplete diffusion and residual nickel, while nanoscale powders can reduce SHS preheat and thermal-explosion ignition temperatures, although agglomeration, oxide content, and pyrophoricity create processing and safety challenges. For Ni3Al, aluminum must remain a continuous phase, with an approximately 2.4:1 Ni-to-Al particle-size ratio; typical useful sizes are about 45 μm Ni and 18 μm Al. In experiments using 3–7 μm nickel, the flame front traversed a 12 mm compact in 0.37 s, followed by intense glowing. Increasing preheat temperature raised combustion temperature and promoted Ni3Al formation. Heating rate also affects ignition control: rapid furnace heating can produce nonuniform surface ignition and loss of process control, whereas the excerpt begins to discuss risks associated with excessively slow heating but is truncated. Because Ti-Al reactions have relatively low exothermicity, conventional ignition by a hot tungsten wire was unsuccessful without preheating; surface reactions could extinguish before becoming self-sustaining. contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant primarily to SHS and thermal-explosion behavior in mechanically activated Al-Ni powder mixtures, but it does not provide data for Al-Ti compacts or a systematic comparison of green density, adiabatic temperature, and reaction hazards. Mechanical milling increases dislocation density, crystallographic defects, powder refinement, and interfacial area. These changes increase powder internal energy, improve diffusion and reaction rates, reduce the ignition barrier, and can shift the reaction from diffusion-controlled to interfacial-controlled behavior. For 3Ni+Al mixtures, prolonged low-energy milling reportedly lowered the thermal-explosion ignition temperature to 400 °C after 50 h. Milling conditions are important: excessive time or energy may produce alloying or reaction products before SHS, whereas insufficient milling may cause heterogeneous deformation and nonuniform grain-size distributions. The excerpt also highlights the influence of compact porosity and processing sequence. Green compacts with density around 0.74–0.76 of theoretical density contain substantial open porosity; vacuum degassing after compaction was associated with significant product porosity, attributed to moisture trapped during mechanical activation. Degassing powders before milling, compaction, and reaction produced substantially lower porosity. Moisture can generate vapor, increase porosity, and slow SHS wave propagation. No explicit adiabatic combustion temperature, ignition-temperature trend versus green density, or discussion of exothermic hazards is given.

For Ti–25 at% Al, Ti–50 at% Al, and Ti–75 at% Al mixtures, relative density affects ignition and propagation through a balance between improved particle contact and excessive thermal conductivity, which can increase heat loss from the reaction zone. The reported optimum green relative density is approximately 60–70%. Finer titanium particles improve titanium–aluminum interfacial contact, shorten diffusion distances, enhance dissolution of solid titanium into molten aluminum, increase reaction-front velocity, and reduce ignition time. Coarser titanium particles generally produce longer ignition times and lower propagation velocities because of reduced interfacial area and greater kinetic resistance, although coarse-grained Ti in TiAl3 showed an atypical behavior attributed to prolonged induction preheating. Combustion temperature varied with composition and particle size, but no clear trend with titanium particle size was identified. The excerpt also notes that TiAl products can show surface-layer melting and peripheral pore accumulation, while TiAl3 has more distributed porosity due to a larger liquid fraction; Ti3Al produced comparatively sound cross sections because less melting occurred.
