contexts.context: The excerpt provides relevant SHS results for pressed Ti-Al powder compacts, but it does not discuss Al-Ni systems directly or explicitly analyze exothermic reaction hazards. Induction heating was used both to preheat and ignite the samples. After ignition, the reaction front propagated downward through the compact, typically requiring about 8–10 seconds, followed by 5–10 seconds of glowing cooling. The reaction caused a rapid temperature rise after electrical power was switched off; the maximum combustion temperature was obtained from temperature-time curves. Combustion temperature increased as green relative density rose from 55% to 65%, attributed to improved particle contact and thermal conductivity. Above 65%, excessive contact enhanced heat loss from the reaction front and reduced combustion temperature. Thus, the highest temperatures generally occurred near 65% relative density. Higher density also increased ignition time because heat was transferred more efficiently away from the heated surface and into surrounding compact layers. Reaction-front velocity was generally optimized at intermediate densities, approximately 65–70% for TiAl and around 60% for TiAl3. contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide specific vacuum hot-pressing or vacuum-sintering processing parameters such as temperature, applied pressure, holding time, or achieved density. It does, however, explain why oxide films and degassing are important during consolidation of aluminum powder. Aluminum powder surfaces can hydrate in water-containing atmospheres; hydroxide layers grow with exposure time and relative humidity, although the measured layers remain thin compared with the approximately 5.0 nm average oxide thickness reported for the studied powders. During heating, degassing removes physically adsorbed water and hydrated oxide products. The cited reactions release water and hydrogen, with hydrogen evolution becoming prominent at roughly 350–400°C. Incomplete removal before consolidation can produce voids and blisters, including potentially during subsequent service. Degassing may also promote oxide-skin breakup through recrystallization reactions, thereby facilitating consolidation. The degassing temperature must balance these effects: excessively low temperatures risk retained water, hydrogen, blistering, and void formation, whereas excessively high temperatures can cause grain growth, precipitate coarsening, or unwanted precipitate formation. The excerpt emphasizes that oxygen distribution and the state of the oxide may matter more than total oxygen content. It contains no direct discussion of vacuum-sintered aluminum compact density or a quantified mechanism for oxide disruption under vacuum hot pressing.

In conventional powder pressing, uniaxial force first rearranges aluminum particles and then plastically deforms them, producing a mechanically bonded green compact. Pure aluminum can reach approximately 90–95% of theoretical density at relatively low pressures, such as 200 MPa; harder prealloyed powders are more difficult to compact. Dry lubricant is added to reduce particle–particle and die-wall friction. During sintering, thermal energy promotes interparticle diffusion and may form a liquid phase. Aluminum sintering temperatures are generally around 600°C, and sintered densities routinely exceed 98% of theoretical. Solid-state sintering is controlled by evaporation-condensation, surface diffusion, volume diffusion, and grain-boundary diffusion, while liquid-phase sintering increases diffusion rates and densification through capillary forces and solution-reprecipitation. Its findings are nevertheless relevant to consolidation mechanisms. For aluminum powders, lower processing temperatures can leave adjacent particles separated by the original refractory oxide film, producing metal/oxide/metal bonding. Increasing temperature improves the elimination or disruption of this layer, while applied mechanical pressure physically breaks down the hard oxide and promotes direct metal/metal bonding. Among the SPS variables examined, ultimate temperature and applied pressure had the largest influence, whereas heating rate and hold time had smaller effects. SPS also reduced residual oxygen and hydrogen substantially compared with atmospheric-pressure molding (APM) counterparts, indicating effective impurity removal or degassing during consolidation under suitable conditions. It does, however, discuss the importance of aluminum’s stable surface oxide film during liquid-phase sintering. In an Al-Sn system, the oxide layer prevents molten tin from contacting metallic aluminum, and the wetting behavior of Sn on Al2O3 can cause tin to be rejected from the compact. Magnesium additions can disrupt or reduce the oxide layer through the reaction 3Mg + 4Al2O3 ⇌ 3MgAl2O4 + 2Al, while also improving liquid-phase wetting; the resulting Sn-rich liquid promotes successful liquid-phase sintering. More generally, liquid-phase sintering proceeds through particle rearrangement, solution-reprecipitation, grain-shape accommodation, and pore elimination, producing faster densification than solid-state sintering. Conventional aluminum powder-metallurgy parts commonly reach approximately 95–99% of theoretical density, leaving residual porosity that reduces ductility and fatigue resistance. contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide specific vacuum hot-pressing temperatures, applied pressures, or a numerical density achieved, nor does it give a detailed account of vacuum sintering of aluminum powder compacts. It does explain the governing mechanisms. Hot pressing or HIP supplies sufficient material flow to disrupt oxide films locally, but generally does not disperse the oxide; mechanical work is therefore needed to break up and redistribute the film so metallic interparticle bonding can form and oxide stringers at prior particle boundaries (PPBs) do not create weak paths. Complete removal of porosity is considered essential because pores act as crack initiation and stress-concentration sites. Degassing should balance gas removal against microstructural degradation, including grain growth and coarsening of intermetallics; excessive temperature can also cause loss of volatile magnesium or zinc. For an Al-Fe-Ce alloy, temperature was the critical parameter: complete degassing required heating to the maximum temperature, while longer treatment at lower temperatures was ineffective. Vacuum is necessary because degassing in air does not fully remove evolved gases. Air-atomized powders can contain hydrated oxide, whereas inert-gas powders mainly have adsorbed water and are easier to degas; re-exposure after degassing causes water readsorption. The excerpt also reports that increasing dynamic-compaction energy increased density and hardness, with evidence of full interparticle bonding in one case.

Increasing applied pressure improved densification and plastic deformation; 50 MPa was selected for subsequent tests. Heating-rate effects were minimal: increasing the rate from 50 to 500 K min−1 raised relative density only from 99.24% to 99.75%, while hardness remained approximately 52 HRH. contexts.context: The excerpt provides experimental context for uniaxial compaction of ECKA Granules Alumix 321, an Al6061-based aluminum powder containing 1.5% Microwax lubricant. Compaction was performed in a 15 mm-diameter, simple single-action die using an Instron hydraulic press, with pressures from 100 to 500 MPa for the characterization curve. Three specimens were produced at each pressure, and their mass, diameter, and height were measured to calculate bulk (green) density. The reported density increased from approximately 2.14 g/cm³ at 100 MPa to approximately 2.57 g/cm³ at 500 MPa, with good repeatability. The procedure also measured the initial powder-column height so that finite-element simulations could use accurate starting dimensions. These details are relevant to studying friction-induced density gradients because the single-action configuration and die-wall contact can produce nonuniform compaction through the specimen height. However, this excerpt does not present direct measurements of density variation from the top to bottom, comparisons across height-to-diameter ratios of 1–3, explicit die-wall friction coefficients, end-capping behavior, or lamination-crack observations. It therefore establishes the material, tooling, loading method, and overall density response, but does not quantify the requested defect or gradient effects.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to die-wall-friction effects on density and stress gradients during metal-powder compaction, although it does not specifically analyze aluminum-only compacts, height-to-diameter ratios of 1–3, end-capping, or lamination cracking. For a Cu–Al mixed powder containing 30 wt% Al, increasing die-wall friction lowers the average relative density and increases the density gradient. The density distributions retain a similar shape at different friction coefficients, but their values differ substantially; reported maximum density differences are 0.0283, 0.1066, and 0.1934 for selected friction conditions. Friction also strongly increases stress nonuniformity, with wider von Mises stress ranges at higher coefficients. In double-action compaction, powder flow is symmetric about the compact mid-plane: axial displacement is greatest near the upper and lower punches and smallest near the middle, indicating load transmission from both ends toward the center. Higher friction reduces axial displacement while making its gradient more pronounced. Radial flow is comparatively small, though it increases with friction; powder near the punches flows toward the center, while powder in the middle flows toward the die wall. The excerpt provides no direct evidence concerning end-capping or lamination cracks.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes experimental and finite-element modeling conditions for axial compaction of Cu–Al mixed metal powder, rather than specifically analyzing die-wall friction, density variation from the top to the bottom, end-capping, or lamination cracking in aluminum compacts. Both single-action and double-action compaction are identified: in single action, the upper punch moves while the die and bottom punch remain stationary; in double action, pressure is applied through both punches. The loading speed was 2 mm/min, followed by a 15-minute dwell at the selected pressure. Density was determined from compact mass and measured volume, with dimensions measured repeatedly using a Vernier caliper. The FE model used MSC.Marc and the modified Shima powder constitutive model, whose parameters depend on relative density. A quarter-cylinder representation of a 3D cylindrical compact was used, with rigid punches and deformable powder. The modeled powder column had an initial height of 40 mm and diameter of 20 mm, corresponding to a height-to-diameter ratio of 2. Two initial relative densities, 0.56 and 0.62, were considered. Although these details provide a relevant geometry and compaction context, the supplied passage does not report wall-friction coefficients, top-to-bottom density gradients, aspect-ratio comparisons from 1 to 3, end-capping behavior, or observed lamination cracks.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns uniaxial die compaction of agglomerated alumina powder rather than aluminum or a metal powder specifically. It establishes that die-wall friction causes incomplete transmission of the applied punch stress through the powder bed, producing stress gradients and non-uniform green-density distributions. These gradients can affect the final sintered shape because density variations lead to differential shrinkage and dimensional distortion. The study experimentally measured density distributions and transmitted stresses, while analytical slice modeling and finite-element analysis were used to predict the resulting stresses and densities. Lubrication condition, compact aspect ratio, and ultimate applied stress were identified as important variables. However, the supplied pages do not provide quantitative density variation from top to bottom for height-to-diameter ratios of 1–3, nor do they specifically discuss end-capping or lamination cracks in pressed aluminum compacts. The excerpt supports the general expectation that increasing wall friction and greater compact height relative to diameter promote stronger stress/density non-uniformity, but it does not establish numerical gradients or crack thresholds for aluminum.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes cold isostatic pressing (CIP) as a process in which powder is enclosed in a flexible mould and compacted by pressurised fluid, rather than by direct uniaxial die loading. The mould must behave like a liquid under high pressure while retaining the required shape at normal pressure. CIP moulds are made from rubber, neoprene, urethane, or other elastomeric materials, and the pressure medium may be oil, water, or glycerine. The stated typical CIP working pressure is 200–400 MPa, with pressure maintained for only a few seconds; for low-compressibility metals, decompression may take several minutes to reduce cracking caused by elastic springback. Because the mould moves with the powder during densification, friction is minimized and pressure acts nearly uniformly from all directions. This produces comparatively uniform density, higher green strength, and allows lower pressure for a given density than die compaction. However, flexible tooling provides less precise dimensional control than rigid die pressing. The excerpt does not distinguish wet-bag from dry-bag CIP, discuss contamination from the bag or fluid, quantify shrinkage, or explain oxide-film disruption mechanisms compared with uniaxial pressing.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a wet-bag cold isostatic pressing (CIP) arrangement rather than a dry-bag system. Aluminum and iron powders were loaded into a flexible, sealed copper tube; the tube was brazed shut and placed in a pressure chamber. Water and mineral oils are identified as possible pressurizing media, while this study used boron oil because it reduced friction and eliminated corrosion. The reported CIP pressure range is not fully detailed, but the specimens were pressed up to 600 MPa. The flexible copper container had a 12.7 mm diameter, 40 mm length, 0.7 mm wall thickness, and 4 cm3 internal volume. Container-volume change during pressing was measured using Archimedes’ principle, and theoretical density was calculated before and after pressing. The introduction states that isostatic pressing promotes uniform shrinkage in all directions. However, this excerpt does not discuss dry-bag CIP, polyurethane, latex, or rubber bags; quantified dimensional tolerances or shrinkage values; contamination from bag materials or pressure fluid; or any mechanism for disrupting oxide films. It also does not compare oxide-film disruption with uniaxial pressing. The principal reported densification result is that Al and Fe reached 98% and 89.2% density, respectively, at 600 MPa before sintering.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes wet-type cold isostatic pressing of iron powder using a flexible natural-rubber mould and a rigid steel mandrel. Powder was filled around a centrally positioned mandrel, vibrated to obtain tap density, covered, sealed against water ingress, and evacuated before pressing. The rubber mould was thin-walled (1 mm) so that its influence on powder densification would be minimized; an aluminum fixture with holes allowed the pressure-transmitting fluid to reach the mould. CIP is presented as capable of producing near-net-shape components with relatively homogeneous and isotropic microstructure, but mandrel–powder friction can disturb powder flow and generate nonuniform density. Smooth and coarse mandrels were compared (surface roughness 0.8 S and 25 S), and friction coefficients were determined from the relationship between compaction pressure and mandrel ejection pressure. contexts.context: The excerpt provides only general powder-compaction information and does not specifically describe cold isostatic pressing (CIP), including wet-bag versus dry-bag procedures, typical CIP pressures, or bag materials such as polyurethane, latex, or rubber. It identifies isostatic pressing as a pressure-based compaction method but gives no process details. More generally, compaction uses external pressure to plastically deform powder into a dense, shaped mass; the resulting density depends on mechanical constraints and pressurization rate. The text explains that compaction initially involves particle rearrangement and, at higher pressures, particle plastic deformation. In the latter stage, oxide films on particles are broken, allowing particle contact and cold welding, which increases green strength and density. This oxide-disruption mechanism is described for powder compaction generally, but the excerpt does not compare it with oxide disruption under isostatic versus uniaxial loading. For uniaxial die pressing, friction at the particle–die-wall interface reduces pressure transmission and produces density gradients; simultaneous upper- and lower-punch pressing improves uniformity. The excerpt also notes that elastic recovery produces radial pressure during ejection and may cause fracture. It reports typical post-compaction densities of 70–90% for conventional cold pressing, but gives no CIP-specific shrinkage, dimensional tolerance, contamination risks from bags or fluid, or pressure ranges. Liquid-phase-sintered aluminum alloys may undergo approximately 1.3–2.5% dimensional change.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a flexible-mold cold isostatic pressing setup for producing a thick-walled iron-powder tube. A 40 mm × 40 mm rubber mold contains a centrally positioned alloy-steel mandrel measuring 40 mm in height and 20 mm in diameter. The iron powder is filled around the mandrel and vibrated to obtain tap density. contexts.context: The study compared air- and nitrogen-atomized Al-alloy powders. Air-atomized powder showed four H₂-release peaks at 175, 290, 335, and 420°C; the first three correlated with water-release peaks. Nitrogen-atomized powder had one clear water/H₂ maximum at higher temperature. For rapidly solidified Al-9Fe-2Mo-1Zr powder, at 550°C “more than 40%” of total hydrogen evolved within 2 min and evolution was “almost completed” after 5 min. Water originated from physically bound moisture and later hydroxide decomposition; hydrogen arose mainly from oxidation/water reaction: **2Al + 3H₂O → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂**. High-vacuum degassing used ~10⁻¹² bar oxygen pressure.
contexts.question:
We make small batches of aluminium-alloy powder by ultrasonic atomization (AMAZEMET rePOWDER, induction-heated module). We are deciding how to turn **pure aluminium powder** (gas-atomized, roughly 15-63 µm, alone or blended with alloying-element or master-alloy powders) into **green parts** that we then melt in the atomizer crucible together with solid alloy (6063 rod, 4047). We want a **pros-and-cons comparison of two consolidation routes**, (A) powder-metallurgy pressing under vacuum and (B) cold isostatic pressing (CIP), judged on **safety** first, then simplicity, speed, cost, and whether the green part will melt, coalesce and mix into the rest of the melt. Please answer from the literature, with citations (DOIs where possible), give numbers wherever the sources have them, and say explicitly which conclusions come from direct evidence for aluminium and which are extrapolated from other metals or from general PM practice.

**Set-up.** Graphite crucible (BN-coated), induction heated, 10-11 cm deep, with a sealing (stopper) rod down the middle; the melt is bottom-poured through a ~0.7 mm hBN nozzle onto a 40 kHz vibrating molybdenum plate. The charge is loaded cold. The chamber is then evacuated and back-filled with argon several times ("gas washes"), including while the charge is held at about 500 °C and still solid. It is then melted under argon at about 0.2 bar overpressure (13-20 ppm O2), set point 810-840 °C, held about 2 minutes (we may extend this to 5-10 minutes), with no mechanical stirring beyond the induction field. Charges are 170-350 g. Every piece must be under 20 mm across to fit between the stopper rod and the crucible wall, so a green part would be a slug about 19 mm in diameter and 20-60 mm long (roughly 10-40 g).

**What we already know** (our own runs, and an earlier literature review on 2026-11-02 that you do not need to repeat). Loose gas-atomized powder sealed in a 6063 cup did not consolidate in one run (AlSi10Mg) and did in another (4047); the oxide shell on each particle, plus MgO or spinel when Mg is present, keeps the molten droplets apart. Cold uniaxial pressing of Al powder reaches about 85 % relative density at about 100 MPa and 92-98 % at 250-580 MPa; it cracks the oxide but does not remove it. Pores start to close above roughly 85-90 % density, so a denser compact can seal in air, adsorbed water and water from hydrated oxide. The equipment maker warned that powder compressed inside a closed aluminium cup could eject molten metal, presumably from trapped gas. Die lubricants add gas and carbon. Cast master alloys, or an arc-melted button made from the weighed powders, were ranked above any pressed compact.

**The two routes to compare.**
- **(A) "Powder metallurgy under vacuum":** uniaxial die pressing with the die cavity evacuated before and during pressing (an evacuable die with a vacuum port and O-ring seals, or a die inside a vacuum chamber or glovebox), with or without vacuum drying or degassing of the loose powder beforehand. Please also cover the natural extensions: pressing followed by vacuum sintering or degassing, and vacuum hot pressing (for example 300-550 °C).
- **(B) Cold isostatic pressing (CIP):** powder filled into a flexible elastomer mould (polyurethane, latex, silicone or rubber bag), optionally evacuated and sealed, and pressed hydrostatically (typically 100-400 MPa) by a water-based fluid or oil. Wet-bag versus dry-bag; buying a small laboratory CIP versus sending parts to a toll-pressing service. Also the combination of A and B: powder vacuum-degassed first, sealed in an evacuated bag, then cold isostatically pressed.

**Please address:**

1. **Pros and cons of each route (and its sub-variants) for pure aluminium powder**, ideally as a table covering: process safety; safety of the green part when melted in our crucible; green density achievable versus pressure, and its uniformity (density gradients and low-density zones in uniaxially pressed slugs with height-to-diameter ratios of about 1-3, versus isostatic pressing); green strength, edge integrity and powder shedding during handling; the need for lubricants and their effect; contamination (lubricant residue, bag material, pressing fluid, die wear); dimensional control (our 20 mm limit, CIP shrinkage and shape tolerance); oxide-film disruption (does hydrostatic loading in CIP break the particle oxide films more or less than the shear in a uniaxial die?); residual gas and moisture in the part; simplicity and the skill needed; time per part and per batch; and cost (equipment capital, tooling and consumables, and toll-service pricing if published).
2. **Which route makes the safer green part to melt in the atomizer, and why.** Quantify where possible: adsorbed and chemically bound water on gas-atomized Al powder (mass %, or mL H2 per 100 g Al) and the temperatures at which it is released; the open-to-closed porosity transition for Al compacts; how much evacuating the die or the CIP bag before pressing reduces the trapped gas; and whether an open-pore green compact heated slowly through our vacuum and argon washes up to about 500 °C would degas in place before its pores close. What are the failure modes: a CIP bag leak or puncture that lets water or oil into the powder (and the hydrogen that water generates with freshly exposed Al), lubricant decomposition, trapped air expanding on heating, lamination or end-capping cracks from uniaxial pressing?
3. **Process hazards of each route** when handling fine pure Al powder: combustible-dust and ignition risks while filling dies or bags, drawing fine powder into a vacuum line or pump, venting an evacuated die to air, contact with the CIP fluid, stored energy in the high-pressure vessel, and safe practice for each (inert handling, filters, grounding, PPE).
4. **Melt-in and mixing feasibility.** Would a green part from either route (at what density) melt, coalesce and mix into a 6063 melt at 810-840 °C under argon within 2-10 minutes with only induction stirring? Does CIP versus uniaxial pressing versus vacuum hot pressing change coalescence, metal yield, dross or oxide inclusions on remelting? Use evidence from remelting Al powder compacts, chip or swarf briquettes, PM parts and foundry alloying tablets. If alloying powders (Si, Cu, Mg, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, Zr) are blended into the pure Al before pressing: segregation while filling, and exothermic reactions between Al and these powders on heating (for example the self-propagating Al-Ni, Al-Ti, Al-Fe or Al-Zr reactions in pressed compacts, and how compact density affects ignition), and whether these help or hurt safety and dissolution.
5. **A practical recipe for each route** for a 19 mm diameter by 20-60 mm slug: pressure, dwell, evacuation level, drying or degassing temperature and time, lubricant (or none), mould or die material and sizing, expected density, and how to check a part before it goes into the crucible (Archimedes density and open porosity, a weight-loss or gas-release test on heating). What press force, or what CIP vessel size and pressure rating, does this need?
6. **Recommendation:** which route, or neither, would you choose for a university lab making a few such parts per week, and when would each be the wrong choice? Compare briefly with buying cast master alloys or arc-melting a button from the weighed powders.

contexts.context: Lee and Kim, *International Journal of Mechanical Sciences* 44 (2002) 1295–1308 (PII S0020-7403(02)00054-1), experimentally studied Al6061 powder under triaxial compression, die compaction, and CIP, validating a finite-element Cap model. They state die-compacted PM parts have “inhomogeneous density distributions” from die-wall friction, causing nonuniform sintering shrinkage and distortion; CIP simulations agreed well with experiments. Their model treats relative density as a hardening parameter and identifies a constitutive transition from rearrangement to plastic densification at relative densities 0.715–0.740. No melting, degassing, oxide, safety, or pure-Al data are provided; extrapolation is therefore necessary.

contexts.context: Estrada, Duszczyk and Korevaar, *J. Mater. Sci.* 26 (1991) 1431–1442 (1991), report that aluminium powder oxide films hydrate, containing physically adsorbed and chemically bound water (hydroxides/oxyhydroxides), hydrogen and oxygen. Vacuum degassing is important before hot consolidation: it removes moisture/hydrogen, decomposes hydrated oxides and converts ductile hydroxide toward brittle γ-alumina; inadequate degassing can cause porosity and blistering. For Al–20Si–X billets up to 550 °C, moisture and hydrogen partial pressures were \(10^{-4}\)–\(10^{-7}\) mbar. MgO shifts release to higher temperatures and reacts with water more intensely than aluminium.

contexts.context: Tang et al. consolidated gas-atomized elemental Al (99.7% and 99.99%) plus <10 µm Al–Cu–Fe alloy powder by **vacuum hot pressing**; composites containing 15, 20, and 30 vol% reinforcement were “fully dense” with “strong interparticle bonding” (Materials Science and Engineering A 383, 362–373, 2004, DOI: **10.1016/j.msea.2004.05.081**). The charge is loaded cold. The chamber is then evacuated and back-filled with argon several times ("gas washes"), including while the charge is held at about 500 °C and still solid. It is then melted under argon at about 0.2 bar overpressure (13-20 ppm O2), set point 810-840 °C, held about 2 minutes (we may extend this to 5-10 minutes), with no mechanical stirring beyond the induction field. Charges are 170-350 g. Every piece must be under 20 mm across to fit between the stopper rod and the crucible wall, so a green part would be a slug about 19 mm in diameter and 20-60 mm long (roughly 10-40 g).

Loose gas-atomized powder sealed in a 6063 cup did not consolidate in one run (AlSi10Mg) and did in another (4047); the oxide shell on each particle, plus MgO or spinel when Mg is present, keeps the molten droplets apart. Cold uniaxial pressing of Al powder reaches about 85 % relative density at about 100 MPa and 92-98 % at 250-580 MPa; it cracks the oxide but does not remove it. Pores start to close above roughly 85-90 % density, so a denser compact can seal in air, adsorbed water and water from hydrated oxide. The equipment maker warned that powder compressed inside a closed aluminium cup could eject molten metal, presumably from trapped gas. Die lubricants add gas and carbon. Cast master alloys, or an arc-melted button made from the weighed powders, were ranked above any pressed compact.

Please also cover the natural extensions: pressing followed by vacuum sintering or degassing, and vacuum hot pressing (for example 300-550 °C).
- **(B) Cold isostatic pressing (CIP):** powder filled into a flexible elastomer mould (polyurethane, latex, silicone or rubber bag), optionally evacuated and sealed, and pressed hydrostatically (typically 100-400 MPa) by a water-based fluid or oil. Also the combination of A and B: powder vacuum-degassed first, sealed in an evacuated bag, then cold isostatically pressed.

Use evidence from remelting Al powder compacts, chip or swarf briquettes, PM parts and foundry alloying tablets. If alloying powders (Si, Cu, Mg, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, Zr) are blended into the pure Al before pressing: segregation while filling, and exothermic reactions between Al and these powders on heating (for example the self-propagating Al-Ni, Al-Ti, Al-Fe or Al-Zr reactions in pressed compacts, and how compact density affects ignition), and whether these help or hurt safety and dissolution.

contexts.context: Tang et al. studied commercial inert-gas-atomized Al (99.7%) and Al–Cu–Fe powders, air-classified below 10 μm. Homogeneous blends were cold-isostatically pressed at **280 MPa**, targeting ~**90% green density**, then machined and vacuum-hot-pressed at **550 °C**, **10⁻⁵ Torr**, for **6 h**, applying **175 or 245 MPa for 5 h**; samples were essentially fully dense. The study notes VHP produces less interparticle shear, strain hardening, and grain anisotropy than quasi-isostatic forging. Thinner oxide surfaces improved tensile properties versus commercial powders with thicker oxide/impurities. This is evidence for Al-based composites, not pure-Al green-part remelting.

(Materials Science and Engineering A 383, 2004, pp. 362–373) consolidated gas-atomized Al powder (<10 μm; 99.99%) with 15–30 vol.% Al–Cu–Fe quasicrystal powder by vacuum hot pressing at 550 °C for 5 h under 175 MPa (after 1 h at 550 °C). XRD showed reaction/transformation to Al₇Cu₂Fe; Al atoms apparently diffused into reinforcement during heating. This is direct aluminium evidence for hot consolidation, not cold pressing, melting, or safety.

Ambient-collected powders were CIPed in 6.35-mm rubber bags at 103.5–138 MPa, achieving 85–95% theoretical density. For <38-µm powder, Bureau-of-Mines MEC classified commercial air/inert-gas powders as “severe,” while GARS powder was “strong”; finer powders were substantially more explosive than 75–106-µm powder.

- **(A) "Powder metallurgy under vacuum":** uniaxial die pressing with the die cavity evacuated before and during pressing (an evacuable die with a vacuum port and O-ring seals, or a die inside a vacuum chamber or glovebox), with or without vacuum drying or degassing of the loose powder beforehand. Please also cover the natural extensions: pressing followed by vacuum sintering or degassing, and vacuum hot pressing (for example 300-550 °C).
- **(B) Cold isostatic pressing (CIP):** powder filled into a flexible elastomer mould (polyurethane, latex, silicone or rubber bag), optionally evacuated and sealed, and pressed hydrostatically (typically 100-400 MPa) by a water-based fluid or oil. Wet-bag versus dry-bag; buying a small laboratory CIP versus sending parts to a toll-pressing service. Also the combination of A and B: powder vacuum-degassed first, sealed in an evacuated bag, then cold isostatically pressed.

**Please address:**

1. **Pros and cons of each route (and its sub-variants) for pure aluminium powder**, ideally as a table covering: process safety; safety of the green part when melted in our crucible; green density achievable versus pressure, and its uniformity (density gradients and low-density zones in uniaxially pressed slugs with height-to-diameter ratios of about 1-3, versus isostatic pressing); green strength, edge integrity and powder shedding during handling; the need for lubricants and their effect; contamination (lubricant residue, bag material, pressing fluid, die wear); dimensional control (our 20 mm limit, CIP shrinkage and shape tolerance); oxide-film disruption (does hydrostatic loading in CIP break the particle oxide films more or less than the shear in a uniaxial die?); residual gas and moisture in the part; simplicity and the skill needed; time per part and per batch; and cost (equipment capital, tooling and consumables, and toll-service pricing if published).
2. **Which route makes the safer green part to melt in the atomizer, and why.** Quantify where possible: adsorbed and chemically bound water on gas-atomized Al powder (mass %, or mL H2 per 100 g Al) and the temperatures at which it is released; the open-to-closed porosity transition for Al compacts; how much evacuating the die or the CIP bag before pressing reduces the trapped gas; and whether an open-pore green compact heated slowly through our vacuum and argon washes up to about 500 °C would degas in place before its pores close. What are the failure modes: a CIP bag leak or puncture that lets water or oil into the powder (and the hydrogen that water generates with freshly exposed Al), lubricant decomposition, trapped air expanding on heating, lamination or end-capping cracks from uniaxial pressing?
3. **Process hazards of each route** when handling fine pure Al powder: combustible-dust and ignition risks while filling dies or bags, drawing fine powder into a vacuum line or pump, venting an evacuated die to air, contact with the CIP fluid, stored energy in the high-pressure vessel, and safe practice for each (inert handling, filters, grounding, PPE).
4. **Melt-in and mixing feasibility.** Would a green part from either route (at what density) melt, coalesce and mix into a 6063 melt at 810-840 °C under argon within 2-10 minutes with only induction stirring? Does CIP versus uniaxial pressing versus vacuum hot pressing change coalescence, metal yield, dross or oxide inclusions on remelting? Use evidence from remelting Al powder compacts, chip or swarf briquettes, PM parts and foundry alloying tablets. If alloying powders (Si, Cu, Mg, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, Zr) are blended into the pure Al before pressing: segregation while filling, and exothermic reactions between Al and these powders on heating (for example the self-propagating Al-Ni, Al-Ti, Al-Fe or Al-Zr reactions in pressed compacts, and how compact density affects ignition), and whether these help or hurt safety and dissolution.
5. **A practical recipe for each route** for a 19 mm diameter by 20-60 mm slug: pressure, dwell, evacuation level, drying or degassing temperature and time, lubricant (or none), mould or die material and sizing, expected density, and how to check a part before it goes into the crucible (Archimedes density and open porosity, a weight-loss or gas-release test on heating). What press force, or what CIP vessel size and pressure rating, does this need?
6. **Recommendation:** which route, or neither, would you choose for a university lab making a few such parts per week, and when would each be the wrong choice? Compare briefly with buying cast master alloys or arc-melting a button from the weighed powders.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: We make small batches of aluminium-alloy powder by ultrasonic atomization (AMAZEMET rePOWDER, induction-heated module). We are deciding how to turn **pure aluminium powder** (gas-atomized, roughly 15-63 µm, alone or blended with alloying-element or master-alloy powders) into **green parts** that we then melt in the atomizer crucible together with solid alloy (6063 rod, 4047). We want a **pros-and-cons comparison of two consolidation routes**, (A) powder-metallurgy pressing under vacuum and (B) cold isostatic pressing (CIP), judged on **safety** first, then simplicity, speed, cost, and whether the green part will melt, coalesce and mix into the rest of the melt. Please answer from the literature, with citations (DOIs where possible), give numbers wherever the sources have them, and say explicitly which conclusions come from direct evidence for aluminium and which are extrapolated from other metals or from general PM practice.

**Set-up.** Graphite crucible (BN-coated), induction heated, 10-11 cm deep, with a sealing (stopper) rod down the middle; the melt is bottom-poured through a ~0.7 mm hBN nozzle onto a 40 kHz vibrating molybdenum plate. The charge is loaded cold. The chamber is then evacuated and back-filled with argon several times ("gas washes"), including while the charge is held at about 500 °C and still solid. It is then melted under argon at about 0.2 bar overpressure (13-20 ppm O2), set point 810-840 °C, held about 2 minutes (we may extend this to 5-10 minutes), with no mechanical stirring beyond the induction field. Charges are 170-350 g. Every piece must be under 20 mm across to fit between the stopper rod and the crucible wall, so a green part would be a slug about 19 mm in diameter and 20-60 mm long (roughly 10-40 g).

**What we already know** (our own runs, and an earlier literature review on 2026-11-02 that you do not need to repeat). Loose gas-atomized powder sealed in a 6063 cup did not consolidate in one run (AlSi10Mg) and did in another (4047); the oxide shell on each particle, plus MgO or spinel when Mg is present, keeps the molten droplets apart. Cold uniaxial pressing of Al powder reaches about 85 % relative density at about 100 MPa and 92-98 % at 250-580 MPa; it cracks the oxide but does not remove it. Pores start to close above roughly 85-90 % density, so a denser compact can seal in air, adsorbed water and water from hydrated oxide. The equipment maker warned that powder compressed inside a closed aluminium cup could eject molten metal, presumably from trapped gas. Die lubricants add gas and carbon. Cast master alloys, or an arc-melted button made from the weighed powders, were ranked above any pressed compact.

**The two routes to compare.**
- **(A) "Powder metallurgy under vacuum":** uniaxial die pressing with the die cavity evacuated before and during pressing (an evacuable die with a vacuum port and O-ring seals, or a die inside a vacuum chamber or glovebox), with or without vacuum drying or degassing of the loose powder beforehand. Please also cover the natural extensions: pressing followed by vacuum sintering or degassing, and vacuum hot pressing (for example 300-550 °C).
- **(B) Cold isostatic pressing (CIP):** powder filled into a flexible elastomer mould (polyurethane, latex, silicone or rubber bag), optionally evacuated and sealed, and pressed hydrostatically (typically 100-400 MPa) by a water-based fluid or oil. Wet-bag versus dry-bag; buying a small laboratory CIP versus sending parts to a toll-pressing service. Also the combination of A and B: powder vacuum-degassed first, sealed in an evacuated bag, then cold isostatically pressed.

**Please address:**

1. **Pros and cons of each route (and its sub-variants) for pure aluminium powder**, ideally as a table covering: process safety; safety of the green part when melted in our crucible; green density achievable versus pressure, and its uniformity (density gradients and low-density zones in uniaxially pressed slugs with height-to-diameter ratios of about 1-3, versus isostatic pressing); green strength, edge integrity and powder shedding during handling; the need for lubricants and their effect; contamination (lubricant residue, bag material, pressing fluid, die wear); dimensional control (our 20 mm limit, CIP shrinkage and shape tolerance); oxide-film disruption (does hydrostatic loading in CIP break the particle oxide films more or less than the shear in a uniaxial die?); residual gas and moisture in the part; simplicity and the skill needed; time per part and per batch; and cost (equipment capital, tooling and consumables, and toll-service pricing if published).
2. **Which route makes the safer green part to melt in the atomizer, and why.** Quantify where possible: adsorbed and chemically bound water on gas-atomized Al powder (mass %, or mL H2 per 100 g Al) and the temperatures at which it is released; the open-to-closed porosity transition for Al compacts; how much evacuating the die or the CIP bag before pressing reduces the trapped gas; and whether an open-pore green compact heated slowly through our vacuum and argon washes up to about 500 °C would degas in place before its pores close. What are the failure modes: a CIP bag leak or puncture that lets water or oil into the powder (and the hydrogen that water generates with freshly exposed Al), lubricant decomposition, trapped air expanding on heating, lamination or end-capping cracks from uniaxial pressing?
3. **Process hazards of each route** when handling fine pure Al powder: combustible-dust and ignition risks while filling dies or bags, drawing fine powder into a vacuum line or pump, venting an evacuated die to air, contact with the CIP fluid, stored energy in the high-pressure vessel, and safe practice for each (inert handling, filters, grounding, PPE).
4. **Melt-in and mixing feasibility.** Would a green part from either route (at what density) melt, coalesce and mix into a 6063 melt at 810-840 °C under argon within 2-10 minutes with only induction stirring? Does CIP versus uniaxial pressing versus vacuum hot pressing change coalescence, metal yield, dross or oxide inclusions on remelting? Use evidence from remelting Al powder compacts, chip or swarf briquettes, PM parts and foundry alloying tablets. If alloying powders (Si, Cu, Mg, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, Zr) are blended into the pure Al before pressing: segregation while filling, and exothermic reactions between Al and these powders on heating (for example the self-propagating Al-Ni, Al-Ti, Al-Fe or Al-Zr reactions in pressed compacts, and how compact density affects ignition), and whether these help or hurt safety and dissolution.
5. **A practical recipe for each route** for a 19 mm diameter by 20-60 mm slug: pressure, dwell, evacuation level, drying or degassing temperature and time, lubricant (or none), mould or die material and sizing, expected density, and how to check a part before it goes into the crucible (Archimedes density and open porosity, a weight-loss or gas-release test on heating). What press force, or what CIP vessel size and pressure rating, does this need?
6. **Recommendation:** which route, or neither, would you choose for a university lab making a few such parts per week, and when would each be the wrong choice? Compare briefly with buying cast master alloys or arc-melting a button from the weighed powders.


## Vacuum-Assisted Uniaxial Die Pressing (Route A) versus Cold Isostatic Pressing (Route B) for Producing Aluminium-Powder Green Parts for Ultrasonic Atomizer Remelting

### 1. Pros-and-Cons Comparison

The following table provides a safety-first, criterion-by-criterion comparison of the two consolidation routes and their sub-variants, based on direct aluminium evidence where available and on general powder-metallurgy practice where noted.

| Criterion | Route A — Vacuum uniaxial pressing | Route B — Cold isostatic pressing (CIP) | Preferred |
|---|---|---|---|
| Process safety during pressing | Powder can remain in an evacuable rigid die or inert glovebox, limiting transfers. Hazards include dust entrainment into the vacuum line, electrostatic ignition, pinch loads, and dust release during venting. Reported Al-powder values span MIE <1–13 mJ, MEC 45–170 g/m³, KSt 162–1100 bar·m/s, and Pmax 8–12.9 bar. Use grounded conductive equipment, filtered vacuum lines, and slow inert-gas venting. (reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 6-7, taveau2019metaldustsexplosion pages 1-2, benson2012safetyconsiderationswhen pages 3-5) | Adds high-pressure stored energy and more powder handling. A punctured wet bag can expose Al to water or oil. Water contacting exposed Al can generate hydrogen by 2Al + 3H₂O → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂. ### 2. Which Route Produces the Safer Green Part to Melt, and Why

**Adsorbed and chemically bound water.** Gas-atomized aluminium powder carries an amorphous hydrated oxide layer approximately 2–10 nm thick (kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 2-4, kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 1-2). Total hydrogen content is typically 13–25 ppm (by weight), equivalent to approximately 14.7–27.5 cm³ H₂ per 100 g of powder, which is 50–100 times higher than that of a degassed casting (estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 6-8). Nearly all of this hydrogen originates from water that is physically adsorbed or chemically bonded as hydroxides in the surface oxide layer (kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 2-4). Physisorbed water is released broadly around 100–200 °C; water associated with hydroxide decomposition (Al₂O₃·3H₂O → Al₂O₃·H₂O → γ-Al₂O₃) evolves over approximately 150–500 °C, with a major transition near 350 °C (623 K) (estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 5-6, yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 2-4, yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 4-4). Hydrogen from the reaction 2Al + 3H₂O → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂ evolves sharply above approximately 350–400 °C and peaks near 450 °C (725 K for pure Al) (yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 2-4, kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 10-11). The optimum vacuum degassing temperature for Al powder consolidation is identified as 623 K (350 °C); for applications requiring minimal blistering, temperatures above 673 K (400 °C) are recommended (yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 4-4).

**Open-to-closed porosity transition.** As aluminium compacts are pressed above approximately 85–90% relative density, pores begin to disconnect and become closed, trapping whatever gas remains inside (meluch2010warmcompactionof pages 45-51). This is the critical safety threshold: a compact pressed to, say, 95% density without prior degassing can seal in air, adsorbed water, and hydroxide-derived hydrogen. When subsequently heated past 350–450 °C, water reacts with freshly exposed aluminium to generate hydrogen gas in a sealed cavity, potentially building enough pressure to eject molten metal—consistent with the equipment maker's warning.

**Evacuating the die versus evacuating the CIP bag.** Evacuating the die cavity to ≤10 mbar before pressing removes approximately 99% of the equilibrated free interstitial gas (atmospheric pressure to 10 mbar represents a 100-fold reduction). However, evacuation does not remove oxide-bound water, which requires thermal treatment. A CIP bag can also be evacuated before sealing, but a sealed but non-evacuated bag merely compresses the original gas inventory. A wet-bag CIP leak introduces water or oil directly into the powder, potentially exposing freshly cracked aluminium surfaces to water—a severe hydrogen-generation hazard (reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 6-7).

**Degassing during the vacuum/argon-wash cycle.** An open-pore green compact (below roughly 85–90% density) heated slowly through the vacuum and argon washes up to 500 °C would indeed lose most of its physisorbed and hydroxide-bound water before pore closure occurs at the melting point, because the dehydration temperatures (100–500 °C) fall well below the aluminium solidus (660 °C). The interconnected porosity at 80–88% density permits gas transport to external surfaces under dynamic vacuum. This is a significant safety advantage over a nearly fully dense compact that cannot degas in situ.

**Failure modes.** Route A's primary failure modes are: (i) pressing too densely without prior degassing, sealing gas inside; (ii) lamination or end-capping cracks from ejection, creating weak zones that may fragment unpredictably during heating; (iii) lubricant decomposition producing gas and carbon if an admixed lubricant is used; and (iv) re-adsorption of moisture between pressing and crucible loading. Route B adds: (v) CIP bag leak or puncture that admits water or oil to the powder, generating hydrogen on freshly exposed Al surfaces; (vi) residual bag or mould-release material contributing organic contamination; and (vii) high-pressure stored-energy release in the event of vessel failure. For the specific application of remelting, **Route A (vacuum-assisted uniaxial pressing) produces the safer green part**, provided the compact is pressed lubricant-free to a moderate density that retains open porosity, and the powder is pre-degassed or the compact is degassed in the atomizer's vacuum/argon-wash cycle before melting.

### 3. Process Hazards

**Aluminium dust explosion characteristics.** Aluminium powder in the 15–63 µm range is classified in Dust Hazard Class 3 (St3), with reported explosion parameters including: minimum ignition energy (MIE) as low as <1 mJ and typically 3–13 mJ; minimum explosible concentration (MEC) of 45–170 g/m³; deflagration index (K_St) of 162–1100 bar·m/s depending on particle size, shape, and test conditions; and maximum explosion pressure (P_max) of 8–12.9 bar (reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 6-7, taveau2019metaldustsexplosion pages 1-2, benson2012safetyconsiderationswhen pages 3-5, cadwallader2003dustcombustionsafety pages 34-38). Metal dust fires cannot be fought with water, CO₂, or nitrogen; only Class D dry-powder agents, dry sand, or dry sodium chloride should be used (cheremisinoff2014dustexplosionand pages 229-232).

**Route A hazards.** Filling an open die generates airborne dust; drawing fine powder into a vacuum line can deposit it in the pump and downstream piping; venting an evacuated die to air disperses fine dust. Mitigation: fill in a fume hood or glovebox under argon; use sintered-metal filters on the vacuum line with an isolation valve; ground all conductive components; vent slowly with dry argon rather than air; wear appropriate PPE including conductive anti-static clothing, safety glasses, and a P3 dust respirator (benson2012safetyconsiderationswhen pages 2-3, cheremisinoff2014dustexplosionand pages 59-63).

**Route B hazards.** CIP adds high-pressure stored energy (a 25 mm bore × 100 mm long vessel at 300 MPa stores substantial elastic energy in the fluid and vessel), requiring a certified vessel, pressure relief, and barricade or blast containment. Bag filling disperses dust; a punctured bag in a water-based system brings water into contact with freshly cracked aluminium powder, generating hydrogen. Mitigation: use oil-based or boron-oil fluid rather than water; double-bag the powder in a glovebox; leak-test the bag before insertion; operate the CIP behind a blast screen; inspect bags and seals after every cycle (eksi2007effectofsintering pages 1-2, kim1998effectoffriction pages 1-2).

**Safe practices common to both routes:** inert-atmosphere handling (argon glovebox or bag-in/bag-out procedure); electrical grounding of all equipment and the operator; anti-static, conductive flooring; filtered local exhaust ventilation; no compressed-air cleaning; housekeeping to prevent dust accumulation; approved storage in sealed conductive containers away from ignition sources (benson2012safetyconsiderationswhen pages 2-3, cheremisinoff2014dustexplosionand pages 59-63).

### 4. Melt-In and Mixing Feasibility

**Remelting evidence.** No study was found that directly reports remelting a pressed pure-aluminium-powder compact into an aluminium melt under the specific conditions described. However, closely analogous evidence exists from aluminium chip/swarf briquettes. Cold-pressed Al–Si–Mg chip briquettes (density 2.29 g/cm³, 12.1% porosity) remelted in an induction furnace at approximately 850 °C achieved a metallurgical yield of 94.2%, with only 2.25% dross, and the resulting casting was chemically homogeneous with no significant segregation (baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 18-20, baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 16-18, baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 20-21). Puga et al. (2009) found that Al swarf briquettes incorporated at 81–85% under argon at 850 °C, with induction melting outperforming resistance melting (83–85% vs 63–69% incorporation), and dross at 10–14% under argon versus 27–35% without protection (puga2009recyclingofaluminium pages 4-5). Higher melting temperatures (up to 950 °C) slightly improved incorporation and reduced melting time from 65 to 50 minutes for their charge sizes.

**Applicability to pressed powder compacts.** A pressed powder compact differs from a chip briquette in having a much higher specific oxide area (each 15–63 µm particle is individually oxide-coated), but the oxide thickness is only 2–10 nm (kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 2-4), much thinner than the heavily oxidised machining chips. In the user's crucible at 810–840 °C under argon with induction stirring, a 10–40 g compact submerged in a 170–350 g melt should heat through its 19 mm cross-section within approximately 1–2 minutes and melt within the 2–10 minute hold. The induction field provides electromagnetic stirring that, while not mechanical, promotes convective mixing. A compact at 85–90% density with open porosity will fragment as aluminium melts and wets inward, liberating individual oxide skins as fine γ-Al₂O₃ particles that should float to the surface as dross. By analogy with briquette remelting, metal yield of approximately 90–95% is a reasonable expectation for a pre-degassed, lubricant-free compact under argon, with the principal loss being oxide-skin dross (extrapolated from chip-briquette data). Achieving yield at the higher end of this range requires minimising re-oxidation during loading and melting.

**CIP versus uniaxial versus vacuum hot pressing.** The consolidation method primarily affects remelting through its influence on residual gas and porosity distribution. A uniformly porous CIP compact and a uniaxially pressed compact with some density gradient should both melt and coalesce, but the CIP compact may break up more uniformly. A vacuum-hot-pressed compact approaching full density would melt in the same manner as a solid piece of aluminium—no gas ejection risk—but vacuum hot pressing at 550 °C and 175–245 MPa for hours is disproportionate effort for a simple remelt feedstock (tanga2004purealmatrix pages 2-3, tanga2004purealmatrix pages 3-5).

**Alloying-powder blends: segregation and exothermic reactions.** If Si, Cu, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, or Zr powders are blended into the Al before pressing, segregation during die filling (density- and size-driven) must be controlled by careful blending and incremental filling. More critically, binary Al–Ni compacts can undergo self-propagating high-temperature synthesis (SHS) with ignition near 640 °C for Ni+Al→Ni₃Al, well below the atomizer melt temperature of 810–840 °C (morsi2026reviewcombustionsynthesis pages 6-7). Al–Ti compacts have a lower exothermicity (adiabatic temperature ~1518 K for TiAl) and may not self-sustain without preheating, but the onset of solid-state reaction is composition- and density-dependent (adeli2016theselfpropagatinghigh pages 1-3, adeli2016theselfpropagatinghigh pages 3-6). The optimal compact green density for SHS is approximately 60–70% of theoretical; higher density improves particle contact and can raise combustion temperature (adeli2016theselfpropagatinghigh pages 3-6, morsi2026reviewcombustionsynthesis pages 6-7). Moisture in compacts promotes porosity and can slow or disrupt the combustion wave (morsi2026reviewcombustionsynthesis pages 9-10). For the user's application, SHS reactions are a potential safety hazard during the slow heating ramp: if the compact reaches the ignition temperature before being submerged in the melt, a runaway exotherm could eject material. **Use of Ni, Ti, Fe, or Zr elemental powders blended with Al in a pressed compact is therefore strongly discouraged for this application.** Master-alloy powders or pre-alloyed powders, where the elements are already in solid solution or as stable intermetallics, do not support SHS and are safer.

### 6. Recommendation

For a university laboratory making a few 19 mm × 20–60 mm aluminium-powder slugs per week for remelting in an ultrasonic atomizer:

**Route A (vacuum-assisted uniaxial die pressing) is recommended over Route B (CIP).** Route A is simpler, requires less capital (a guarded hydraulic press, hardened die, and vacuum hardware versus a certified high-pressure CIP vessel and ancillaries), introduces no fluid-contact failure mode, and provides better dimensional control for the tight 19 mm clearance. With lubricant-free pressing at 200–300 MPa after vacuum drying of the powder, targeting 85–90% theoretical density with retained open porosity, the compact can degas in situ during the atomizer's vacuum and argon-wash cycles before its pores close at the melting point. The compact should be pressed as short slugs (H/D ≤ 1.5, i.e. ≤ 28 mm long) using double-action punches to minimise density gradients (wang2018numericalsimulationof pages 16-22, beck2012onanovel pages 20-26). Every slug should be verified by Archimedes density and a go/no-go gauge before loading.

**When Route A is the wrong choice:** (i) if a tall slug (H/D > 2) is required and density uniformity is critical—CIP is then better for structural uniformity, but use pre-degassed powder in a dry evacuated bag; (ii) if the laboratory already has access to a CIP facility or toll-pressing service and not a suitable press, sending occasional parts out for CIP may be faster than building tooling in-house.

**When Route B is the wrong choice:** (i) if no CIP facility is available and the cost of a vessel is not justified for a few parts per week; (ii) if only water-based CIP fluid is available, because any bag leak exposes Al powder to water; (iii) if the operator cannot reliably verify bag integrity and vacuum seal before and after pressing.

**When neither route is the best choice:** Cast master alloys or an arc-melted button from the weighed elemental charges remain safer and more reliable than any green pressed compact. A fully pre-melted and solidified charge piece contains no trapped gas, no adsorbed water, no individual particle oxide shells, and no risk of powder ejection—it simply remelts. The trade-off is that arc melting requires an arc furnace and produces only one composition per melt, while pressing is a room-temperature process that can incorporate custom powder blends. For standard alloy compositions (6063, 4047) where commercial master alloys are available, the recommendation is to **prefer cast or arc-melted charge pieces over either pressed-powder route**, and to reserve powder pressing for compositions where no suitable master alloy exists and where the added risks can be justified and managed.

### Evidence Basis and Limitations

Direct aluminium-specific evidence is available for: green density versus pressure in CIP (eksi2007effectofsintering pages 1-2, andasmas2011phenomenologicalstudyof pages 2-4); degassing temperatures and hydrogen content of gas-atomised Al powder (yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 2-4, yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 4-4, estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 6-8, kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 2-4, estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 5-6, kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 7-8); Al-powder explosion parameters (reding2018metaldustexplosion pages 6-7, taveau2019metaldustsexplosion pages 1-2, benson2012safetyconsiderationswhen pages 3-5); SHS ignition in Al–Ni and Al–Ti compacts (morsi2026reviewcombustionsynthesis pages 6-7, adeli2016theselfpropagatinghigh pages 3-6); vacuum hot pressing of Al composites (tanga2004purealmatrix pages 2-3, tanga2004purealmatrix pages 3-5); and remelting of Al chip briquettes (puga2009recyclingofaluminium pages 4-5, baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 18-20, baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 16-18). Density-gradient data for uniaxially pressed compacts at various H/D ratios are extrapolated from Cu–Al mixed-powder simulations (wang2018numericalsimulationof pages 16-22, wang2018numericalsimulationof pages 6-9); general CIP descriptions are from PM textbook-level sources applied to aluminium (meluch2010warmcompactionof pages 51-58, beck2012onanovel pages 20-26); and the specific behavior of a pressed Al-powder green compact during remelting in a small induction-heated crucible has not been directly studied in the published literature and is inferred from briquette remelting studies and PM degassing work. The oxide-disruption mechanism in CIP versus uniaxial pressing for pure aluminium powder has not been experimentally compared in any study identified in this review; the conclusion that uniaxial pressing introduces slightly more shear-induced oxide cracking is a reasonable inference from general PM principles but is not validated for this system.

| Criterion | Route A — Vacuum uniaxial pressing | Route B — Cold isostatic pressing (CIP) | Preferred |
|---|---|---|---|
| Process safety during pressing | Powder can remain in an evacuable rigid die or inert glovebox, limiting transfers. Hazards include dust entrainment into the vacuum line, electrostatic ignition, pinch loads, and dust release during venting. Reported Al-powder values span MIE <1–13 mJ, MEC 45–170 g/m³, KSt 162–1100 bar·m/s, and Pmax 8–12.9 bar. Use grounded conductive equipment, filtered vacuum lines, and slow inert-gas venting. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029) | Adds high-pressure stored energy and more powder handling. A punctured wet bag can expose Al to water or oil. Water contacting exposed Al can generate hydrogen by 2Al + 3H₂O → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂. Use an evacuated, leak-tested, double-contained bag and an oil rather than water medium where practicable. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000057) | **A**, if engineered for combustible metal powder. |
| Safety of green part during remelting | Evacuating the loose bed before pressing removes much free pore gas, but high-density pressing can isolate remaining air, water, or lubricant. A lubricant-free, measurably open-pore compact that is slowly heated under dynamic vacuum is preferable to a nearly closed, un-degassed compact. | An evacuated dry bag can remove free gas before densification and CIP avoids weak low-density zones. A leaking wet bag can introduce water or oil; a sealed but non-evacuated bag merely compresses the original gas. | **A by default**; **B only with an evacuated, dry, leak-tested bag**. |
| Green density achievable | Direct Al-alloy evidence: single-action pressing produced about 2.14 g/cm³ at 100 MPa and 2.57 g/cm³ at 500 MPa. That powder contained lubricant, so it is not a pure-Al calibration. Vacuum changes gas inventory more than the pressure–density curve. (pqac-00000053) | Direct Al evidence: initial packing near 48% theoretical density reached 98% at 600 MPa; other pure-Al/Al–Ni work exceeded 95% at sufficiently high pressure. Typical CIP practice is 200–400 MPa. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000054) | **B** for maximum density, although maximum density before degassing is not the safest target. |
| Density uniformity | Die-wall friction attenuates pressure. Single-action pressing leaves the remote end least dense; double-action pressing moves the minimum toward mid-height. In Cu–Al compacts, raising H/D from 0.7 to 2.12 increased maximum relative-density difference from 0.0851 to 0.1206; application to pure Al is an extrapolation. (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000052) | Hydrostatic loading and the moving elastomer wall provide much better uniformity. Direct Al–Ni/pure-Al work found that a 1 min pressure dwell produced good homogeneity, whereas immediate decompression produced a dense surface and lower-density core. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005) | **B**, especially for long slugs with H/D around 2–3. |
| Green strength, edge integrity, and shedding | Good at adequate pressure, but tall slugs are vulnerable to laminations, end-capping, weak central regions, and ejection damage. Rigid tooling gives clean edges. | Usually higher and more uniform handling strength, without rigid-die ejection. Bag wrinkles and rounded edges are possible; slow decompression may be needed to prevent springback cracking. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000058) | **B** for handling; **A** for precise edges. |
| Lubricant need and contamination | Die friction encourages lubricant use, but internal wax or stearate adds carbon and gas. For remelting, use no admixed lubricant; if unavoidable, apply the minimum external die-wall film and validate its removal. | Normally needs no internal lubricant because the bag moves with the powder, avoiding wax decomposition and carbon pickup. | **B**. |
| Bag or pressure-fluid contamination | No bag or pressure fluid. Possible contamination comes from die wear, vacuum grease, O-rings, pump backstreaming, or external die lubricant. | Possible elastomer fragments, mould-release residue, oil permeation, or catastrophic fluid ingress. Literature describes rubber, neoprene, or urethane moulds with water, oil, glycerine, or boron oil. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000057) | **A**. |
| Oxide-film disruption | Axial plastic flow and die-wall shear can crack native oxide locally, but do not remove it. | Hydrostatic compression deforms particles but produces less macroscopic shear. It probably fractures oxide at contacts, but direct evidence that ordinary CIP disrupts pure-Al oxide more effectively than die pressing was not found. | **A, slightly**, for cold oxide cracking; the distinction is uncertain. |
| Residual gas and moisture | Direct evacuation of the loose bed removes free interstitial gas. Al powders have shown about 13–25 ppm H, equivalent to approximately 14.7–27.5 cm³ H₂ per 100 g, mainly associated with water on the oxide. Physisorbed water evolves mainly near 100–200°C; hydroxide-related water and H₂ evolve broadly through 200–450°C. Hydrated oxide transforms near 350°C (623 K). (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000067, pqac-00000069) | Evacuating the bag removes free gas but not oxide-bound water. Fluid exposure can add moisture after drying. A non-evacuated bag traps the initial gas inventory. | **A**, unless B uses vacuum-degassed powder and dry evacuated-bag sealing. |
| Dimensional control and 20 mm limit | Best control. A nominal 19 mm rigid die produces a near-final diameter; springback should be calibrated and every slug checked with a go/no-go gauge. | Flexible-tool shrinkage depends on fill density, bag stiffness, closure geometry, and powder flow. Curvature, taper, and wrinkles are possible, and oversize mould dimensions must be established experimentally. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000056) | **A**. |
| Simplicity and skill | Straightforward if a guarded press exists, although vacuum ports, filters, inert venting, seals, and preferably double-action tooling add complexity. | Wet-bag CIP requires bag filling, evacuation, sealing, vessel loading, pressure cycling, controlled decompression, stripping, and leak inspection. Dry-bag equipment is faster but difficult to justify for a few parts weekly. | **A** in a university laboratory; toll CIP is preferable to buying a unit for trials. |
| Time per part or batch | Filling, evacuation, pressing, decompression, and ejection can take minutes. Several short slugs are easier than one H/D≈3 slug. Separate thermal degassing dominates total time. | Pressure hold may be seconds to 1 min, but bag preparation and vessel cycling dominate; decompression may take several minutes. Several bags can be processed together. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000054) | **A** for one-offs; **B** for batches. |
| Equipment capital and consumables | Lowest likely capital if a hydraulic press is available. Requires a hardened die, punches, vacuum hardware, filtration, and guarded/inert venting. Rigid tooling has low recurring consumable cost. | A 200–400 MPa vessel, intensifier, interlocked enclosure, inspection program, and disposable bags impose substantial capital and operating cost. Wet-bag tooling is cheaper but labor intensive. No reliable published toll-service price was found. | **A**; use toll CIP for occasional development work. |
| Vacuum sintering or post-press degassing | A lubricant-free compact can be heated under vacuum while pores remain connected, but vacuum sintering alone cannot remove stable Al₂O₃. Degassing near 350°C is supported for hydrated-oxide conversion; higher temperatures risk pore closure and volatile-alloy-element loss. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040) | Post-CIP degassing is possible, but very high density can reduce gas pathways. Degassing loose powder before CIP is preferable. | **A**, or pre-degassed evacuated-bag CIP. |
| Vacuum hot pressing extension | Direct Al-composite evidence: about 90%-dense CIP preforms were hot pressed at 550°C, 10⁻⁵ Torr, and 175–245 MPa for 5 h, producing essentially full density. This improves bonding and degassing but is slow and unnecessary for simple remelt feed. (pqac-00000064, pqac-00000065) | CIP can provide a uniform preform before vacuum hot pressing, but this is no longer a simple cold-CIP route. | **Neither for routine feedstock**. |
| Overall recommendation | Best practical cold route for a few parts per week: lubricant-free, double-action vacuum die pressing of short slugs after controlled vacuum drying or degassing, targeting adequate strength with retained open porosity rather than maximum density. | Best cold route for density uniformity and low shedding, but only with pre-degassed powder, a dry evacuated double bag, controlled decompression, and rejection after any suspected leak or fluid contact. | **A over B**, but cast master alloy or an arc-melted button remains safer and more reliable than either green compact. |


*Table: Safety-first comparison of vacuum-assisted uniaxial pressing and CIP for producing aluminium-powder slugs for remelting. Direct aluminium evidence is quantified where available, with other conclusions identified through their cited PM analogies.*

Begin with an internal former around 21–24 mm diameter and determine experimentally the oversize needed to obtain ≤19 mm after shrinkage. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000057) |
| Target green density | Target 85–90% theoretical density, equivalent to 2.30–2.43 g/cm³ for pure Al, provided measurable open porosity remains. Do not maximize density before degassing. | Target 85–90% theoretical density. If handling requires 90–95%, use only pre-degassed powder in an evacuated bag and verify gas release independently. CIP can exceed 95% at high pressure. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002) |
| Expected density and mass | At 200–300 MPa, an initial development expectation is about 2.25–2.45 g/cm³, subject to powder and tooling. At 19 mm diameter this corresponds to approximately 13–14 g at 20 mm length, 26–28 g at 40 mm, and 39–42 g at 60 mm. | At 150–250 MPa, expect approximately 2.30–2.50 g/cm³, but establish a pressure–density curve for the actual powder. Pure Al achieved 85–95% density at 103.5–138 MPa in one study and 98% at 600 MPa in another. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000063) |
| Decompression / ejection | Reduce load over 30–60 s and pause at low load before full release. Eject slowly with a supported lower punch. Inspect for end-capping, circumferential laminations, and cracks at the middle or remote end. | Decompress over at least 1–3 min and lengthen the cycle if springback cracks occur. Keep the bag contained until external fluid has been removed, then strip it over a clean tray. Low-compressibility metals may require several minutes. (pqac-00000054) |
| Dimensional acceptance | Require diameter ≤19.0 mm everywhere using a go/no-go gauge. Prefer 20–30 mm lengths. In Cu–Al compacts, increasing H/D from 0.7 to 2.12 increased maximum relative-density variation from 0.0851 to 0.1206; application to pure Al is an extrapolation. (pqac-00000046) | Require diameter ≤19.0 mm everywhere after bag removal. Reject folds, necking, taper, and closure-end bulges. Flexible-tool shrinkage must be calibrated for each bag and filling procedure. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000056) |
| Density and porosity check | Record mass, dimensions, and geometric density. Determine open porosity with a validated nonreactive immersion liquid followed by complete drying, or use helium pycnometry plus envelope density. Require batch density within ±2% relative and connected porosity if relying on in-crucible degassing. | Apply the same tests. Compare dimensions before and after CIP to detect abnormal bag restraint or leakage. During qualification, section slugs and compare top, middle, and bottom density. |
| Thermal qualification | Heat a sacrificial slug under the intended dynamic-vacuum ramp to 500°C while recording mass and pressure, preferably with H₂O/H₂ residual-gas analysis. Require reproducible mass loss and no pressure spike, swelling, cracking, spalling, or ejection. Al powders have shown about 13–25 ppm H, equivalent to 14.7–27.5 cm³ H₂ per 100 g. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000066, pqac-00000069) | Use the same qualification. Reject a part if its bag lost vacuum, changed mass unexpectedly, showed wetting or discoloration, or either containment layer was damaged. A leak into water-based fluid is disqualifying and should not be corrected by redrying. |
| Key warnings | Fit vacuum lines with grounding, a metal-powder trap, an isolation valve, and pump protection. Never vent an evacuated powder-filled die rapidly to air. Avoid moist powder, internal lubricants, tall single-action compacts, and near-full densification before degassing. Al-powder MIE can be below 1–13 mJ. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000029) | CIP adds high-pressure stored energy and a fluid-ingress failure mode. Treat either water or oil ingress as rejection. Freshly exposed Al can generate H₂ according to 2Al + 3H₂O → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂. (pqac-00000022) |


*Table: Safety-first starting recipes for producing 19 mm diameter aluminium-powder slugs by vacuum die pressing or evacuated-bag CIP. Values requiring qualification on the actual powder and equipment are presented as development ranges rather than validated production limits.*
